ŚŚS 14.63.1: The *ṛṣistoma*s. ŚŚS 14.63.2: Gotama, desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), performed austerities and perceived this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*).
By means of this, having sacrificed, one obtains spiritual luster (*brahman-varcasa*); therefore, one who desires spiritual luster should sacrifice with it.
Bharadvāja, desiring strength, performed austerities and perceived this sacrificial rite (*yajña-kratu*).
By means of it, having sacrificed, one obtains strength;
therefore, one who desires strength should sacrifice with it.
Atri, desiring offspring, performed austerities and perceived this sacrificial rite.
Having sacrificed with it, he procreated;
therefore, one who desires offspring should sacrifice with it.
Vasiṣṭha, desiring the consumption of food, performed austerities and perceived this sacrificial rite.
By means of that, having sacrificed, one obtains food;
therefore, one who desires food should sacrifice with it.
Jamadagni, desiring cattle, performed austerities and perceived this sacrificial rite.
By means of it, having sacrificed, one obtains cattle;
therefore, one who desires cattle should sacrifice with it.
Prajāpati, desiring offspring, performed austerities and beheld this sacrificial rite.
Having sacrificed with that, he procreated;
therefore, one who desires offspring should sacrifice with it.
The days of the *pṛṣṭhya* [six-day rite] follow in their proper sequence.
The Vrātya-stomas.
The Vasus, desiring heaven, performed austerities and perceived these sacrificial rites, the Vrātya-stomas. Having sacrificed with them, they attained heaven.
One who desires heaven should sacrifice with these [offerings]:
to Mitra and Varuṇa, to the Aśvins, to the Vasus, to the Maruts, and to the Viśvedevas.
The recitation (śastra) follows the Pṛṣṭhya Śastra from which it has been drawn.
The *utkrānti* is an *atirātra*.
Indra and Viṣṇu, desiring the heavenly world, performed austerities and beheld this sacrificial rite, the *utkrānti*. Having sacrificed with it, they ascended to the heavenly world.
"One desiring heaven should sacrifice with this [sacrifice].
At the insertion of the *nivid*, [the verses] "These [songs], O Indra" and "He who, like the sky...

[are used]. "Forward to Pūṣan, Viṣṇu, Agni, the wise one," and "O drinker of the dregs, acting together with Viṣṇu"—these are the *viṣṇunyaṅga* verses; they constitute the characteristic form (*rūpa*) of this day.
Of Mitra and Varuṇa, of the Aśvins, of the Vasus, of the Maruts, of the Sādhyas, of the Āpyas, of the Viśvasṛjs, of the Bhūtakrts, and of those who are eldest, middlemost, and youngest;
the Caturdaśa-stoma is [the fee].
The gift is a wide-spreading chariot with a goad, together with arrows and a bow.
The *śastra* for these groups of deities follows from the *samūḷha-daśarātra*.
[It applies] to the *vrātyastomas*,
and to the nine *nākasads*.

[And there are the offerings] of the *caṣāla*, the *mukha-tarasa*, the *puroḍāśa*, the *vaniṣṭu-sava*, the *brahma-sava*, the *kṣatra-sava*, the *bhūmi-sava*, the *oṣadhi-sava*, the *odana-sava*, and the *vanaspati-sava*.
Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin, desiring a firm foundation, performed austerity and beheld this tenth day as a sacrificial rite (*yajña-kratu*). Having sacrificed with it, he became firmly established.
One who desires a firm foundation should sacrifice with these.
These are the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtustoma*).
Indeed, the seasons, desiring heaven, performed austerities and perceived these six sacrificial rites.
Having sacrificed with them, they attained heaven;
one who desires heaven should sacrifice with them.
These are the month-stomas (māsa-stoma).
Those who desired food and sustenance performed austerities and beheld these twelve sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*).
Having sacrificed with them, they obtained food and sustenance. One who desires food and sustenance should sacrifice with them.
The *ardhamāsa-stomas*.
Indeed, those desiring food and drink, having performed austerities, beheld these twenty-four sacrificial rites (*yajña-kratus*);
having sacrificed with them, they obtained food and drink.
One who desires food and other such things should sacrifice with these. These are the Nakṣatra-stomas.
Having performed austerities, those desiring splendor perceived these twenty-seven sacrificial rites, which are the Nakṣatras.
Having sacrificed with them, they attained splendor (*tejas*). One who desires splendor should sacrifice with them.
These are the *ahorātrastoma* sacrifices.
Those who desired food and other enjoyments performed austerities and beheld these sacrificial rites numbering twenty-seven hundred.
Having sacrificed with them, they obtained food and enjoyments. One who desires food and enjoyments should sacrifice with them.

The *muhūrta-stomas*. Those who desired food and sustenance performed austerities and beheld these sacrificial rites (*yajña-kratūn*): ten thousand and eight hundred. Having sacrificed with them, they obtained food and sustenance.
One who desires food and other provisions should sacrifice with these. These are the Nimeṣa-stomas.
Having performed austerities, the Nimeṣas—desiring imperishability—beheld these sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*), numbering one hundred and eight thousand.
Having sacrificed with them, they attained imperishability; one who desires imperishability should sacrifice with them. These are the *dhvaṃsi-stomas*.

Those of infinite desire, having performed austerities, beheld these sacrificial rites—ten million and eight hundred thousand of them. By performing sacrifices with them, they attained the infinite. One who desires the infinite should sacrifice with them.
The Diśām-stomas. Regarding the Diśām-stomas:
the quarters (diśas), desiring infinity, performed austerities and beheld these four sacrificial rites (yajña-kratus). Having sacrificed with them, they attained infinity.
One who desires infinity should sacrifice with these.
(ŚŚS 14.84.1) These are the Stomas of the intermediate directions.
(ŚŚS 14.84.2) Desiring infinity, the intermediate directions performed austerities and beheld these four sacrificial rites.
Having sacrificed with these, they attained the infinite;
one who desires the infinite should sacrifice with them.
These [sacrifices] should have the Bṛhat and Rathantara as their Pṛṣṭha-stotras.
ŚŚS 14.84.4: [The rites] have the *śastra* recitations performed on a single day.
ŚŚS 14.84.5: At the insertion of the *nivid*, either the *kayāśubhīya* or the *tadidāsīya* [sāmans are used].
ŚŚS 14.84.6: The *stomas* of the cardinal directions are in the cardinal directions, and those of the intermediate directions are in the intermediate directions.
ŚŚS 15.1.1: The Vājapeya sacrifice is performed in autumn.
ŚŚS 15.1.2: It is for one who desires food and nourishment.
ŚŚS 15.1.3: One who is about to sacrifice with the Vājapeya first performs sacrifices consisting of libations for one year.
ŚŚS 15.1.4: Drink, indeed, is the peyās;
food is the vāja.
ŚŚS 15.1.5: Drink comes first, and then food.
For the attainment of both of these:
there are twelve Agniṣṭomas;
or, according to Gotama, the four-increasing stoma is performed alternately with the original one.
ŚŚS 15.1.9: Some [say] it is a sacrifice without a patron.
ŚŚS 15.1.10: Having sacrificed with this sacrificial rite, Indra and Bṛhaspati obtained food to eat.
ŚŚS 15.1.11: One who desires food should sacrifice with that [rite].
Now, by this [rite], there are three days of consecration (dīkṣā), three days of preparatory offerings (upasad), and the Soma-pressing day as the seventeenth.
For Prajāpati is seventeenfold, and the Vājapeya is [identical with] Prajāpati;
thus he causes him to prosper in his own form.

The sacrificial post is made of Bilva wood, fourteen cubits long, with four corners, and its smoke-receptacle is shaped like a cow’s tail. Prajāpati is seventeenfold, and the Vājapeya sacrifice is seventeenfold;
thus, it endows him with his own form.

ŚŚS 15.1.19: There are seventeen [animals] dedicated to Agni and Soma. ŚŚS 15.1.20: Their ritual procedure is the same. ŚŚS 15.1.21: [The first is] for Agni; [the second] for Indra and Agni; [the third] is a bull for Indra.
A ewe for Sarasvatī;
a speckled cow for the Maruts who are victorious; the fifth is among the animals of the *kratu* sacrifices.
Seventeen dark-colored hornless goats with dewlaps are to be offered to Prajāpati.
ŚŚS 15.1.23: For the *savanīya* offerings, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) extends up to the *paryagni-karaṇa*.
ŚŚS 15.1.24: They are sacrificed to with the *brahmasāman*.
ŚŚS 15.1.25: The *ādhrigu* formula and the *stokyās* should be repeated.
ŚŚS 15.1.26: "Bring fire for him; bring the omentum-eating [fire]"—this is the *tantra* (the common framework) for the final *prayāja* and the two *parivāpya* offerings.
ŚŚS 15.1.27: The offering after the *hāriyojana* cup follows.
ŚŚS 15.1.28: The subsidiary rites beginning with the *vanaspati* offering may be postponed.
ŚŚS 15.1.29: Or [it is performed] during the *anuyāja* offerings when they have been completed. ŚŚS 15.1.30: Or [it is performed] at its own proper time.
ŚŚS 15.1.31: It has the seventeenfold hymn-form (*saptadaśastoma*).
The Ājya-stotra is the Vairāja;
or it is the Ghṛtastomīya;
the Praüga-śastra belongs to Mādhucchandas.
The Virāj is indeed food;
ghee is its food.
The Mādhucchandasa Praüga is the essence.
ŚŚS 15.1.37: By means of food, one bestows its essence.
ŚŚS 15.1.38: Or it is a one-day rite (aikāhika).
ŚŚS 15.1.39: For the one-day rite is a firm foundation (pratiṣṭhā).
ŚŚS 15.1.40: It is for the sake of stability alone.
ŚŚS 15.2.1: With the *aticchandas* verse, "In the *trikadruka*s, the buffalo [drinks] the barley-mash, O thou of great strength," he begins the *marutvatīya* litany.
ŚŚS 15.2.2: The *aticchandas* meter indeed belongs to Prajāpati.
Prajāpati is the Vājapeya;
thus it endows him with his own form.
One should begin with the verse: "Like a chariot, for our protection... (RV 8.68.1).
The *anuṣṭubh* metre belongs to Prajāpati;
the Vājapeya sacrifice is Prajāpati;
thus, he causes him to prosper through his own form.
ŚŚS 15.2.9: "With what [splendor]? and "The beautiful ones, of equal age, dwelling together"—these constitute the *marutvatīya* [śastra]. The *kayāśubhīya* [sāman] contains the word *ka*.
ŚŚS 15.2.10: Prajāpati is indeed Vājapeya; [the sacrifice] is characterized by the syllable *ka*.
Thus, he causes him to prosper in his own form.
There is an offering of wild rice (*naivāra*) for Bṛhaspati, consisting of seventeen *śarāva* measures.
Prajāpati, indeed, is seventeenfold, as is the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Thus, he causes him to prosper in his own form.
This occurs between the Niṣkevalya and the Marutvatīya,
and at the Bṛhaspatisava.
ŚŚS 15.2.16: Therein, he is consecrated prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. ŚŚS 15.2.17: Its presentation consists of the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā*.
ŚŚS 15.2.18: "This indeed was the foremost among beings"—this is the *niṣkevalya* hymn.
The sacrifice is indeed the eldest among the worlds;
the Vājapeya is indeed Prajāpati, the sacrifice.
Thus, he causes him to prosper through his own form.
ŚŚS 15.2.22: From the *anucara* onwards, up to the sixth [verse], belongs to the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*).
ŚŚS 15.2.23: Indeed, the sixth day is dedicated to Prajāpati.
ŚŚS 15.2.24: Prajāpati is the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Thus it endows him with his own form;
or [it may be done] at the Viṣuvat;
for the Viṣuvat is indeed an ascent.
The Vājapeya is a growth.
It thus endows it with its own form.
Or it is a one-day sacrifice (aikāhika).
ŚŚS 15.2.31: The one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) is indeed a firm foundation.
ŚŚS 15.2.32: It is for the sake of stability alone.

Therefore, one should sacrifice with the Catuṣṭoma alone;
for the Catuṣṭoma is the firm foundation of sacrifices.
It is for the sake of stability alone.
Ten thousand is the sacrificial fee.
Indeed, neither from his kingdom nor from that community does anyone turn away who gives ten thousand.
That is the "ten-thousandfold" nature of the ten thousand.
Or, it is a hundred thousand.
King Hariścandra, the son of Vidhaśa and of the Ikṣvāku lineage, was childless.
He had a hundred wives, yet he did not obtain a son through them. Parvata and Nārada lived in his house; he questioned Nārada.
"O Nārada, tell us this: what is it that those who desire a son, both those who know him and those who do not, seek to obtain through a son? Thus [he asked].
When questioned with one [verse], he replied with ten: "In this [son] the father pays his debt and finds immortality, if he sees the face of the son born alive. ŚŚS 15.17.1c.
Whatever enjoyments there are on earth, whatever exist in Jātavedas,
and whatever belong to living beings in the waters— greater than all those combined is the father’s [joy] in his son.
Through a son, the ancestors have forever crossed over the thick darkness.
For the Self was born from the Self; it is the one that is nourishing and carries one across.
What indeed is the use of the antelope skin, what the use of the beard, and what the use of ascetic toil?
O seekers of Brahman, desire a son; he indeed is the world that cannot be blamed.

Food is indeed breath; clothing is refuge; gold is beauty; cattle are marriages; a friend is a wife; a daughter is a source of pity; and a son is light in the highest heaven. Let the husband enter his wife, becoming an embryo, and then [enter] the mother.

Having become new again within her, he is born in the tenth month. Therefore, she is called "jāyā" (wife), because he is born (*jāyate*) from her again. This is his manifestation; this seed is deposited as his manifestation.
Both the gods and the seers gathered this great splendor together.
The gods said to men: "This is your mother once again;
this is the extended path traveled by the gods, by which those who possess sons and are free from sorrow ascend."
Beasts and birds behold it; therefore they even engage in sexual union with their mothers.
All beasts know this: "There is no world for one who has no son.
Therefore, a son mounts his mother and his sister.
He said,
"Tell me how a son may be born to me.
He spoke to him.
"Go for refuge to King Varuṇa, saying: 'May a son be born to me; with him I shall sacrifice to you.
"So be it. He then went to King Varuṇa.
"May a son be born to me; with him I shall sacrifice for you. "So be it," [he replied].
A son was born to him, named Rohita.
Varuṇa said to him:
"A son has indeed been born to you; sacrifice to me with this. He replied:
"When an animal has passed ten days, then it becomes fit for sacrifice. Let it first pass ten days, and then I shall sacrifice to you."
"So be it," he replied.
He remained [in that state] for ten days.
Then he said to him:
"Or rather, let him be one whose ten-day period has passed; sacrifice with this [animal].
He replied, "When the teeth of an animal have grown, then it becomes fit for sacrifice. Let his teeth grow first, and then I shall sacrifice for you."
"So be it," he said. His teeth grew.
He said to him:
"His teeth have indeed grown; sacrifice with this."
He said:
"When the teeth of an animal grow back again, then it becomes fit for sacrifice. Let his teeth grow back again; then I shall sacrifice you. "So be it," he replied. And his teeth grew back again.
He said to him:
"His teeth have grown back again; sacrifice with this [wealth].
He replied.

"When a Kṣatriya puts on his armor, he then becomes fit for sacrifice; he becomes fit for sacrifice once he has put on his armor. Let him first put on his armor, and then I shall sacrifice for you. "So be it," he replied. He then put on his armor. [The other] said to him:
"He has indeed put on his armor; sacrifice for me with this man! Having said, "So be it," he addressed his son:
"This man has indeed given you to me; come, let me sacrifice with you."
Having said, "So be it," he took up his bow and retired to the forest.
He wandered in the forest for a year.
Then Varuṇa seized the king of the Ikṣvākus.
A tumor arose on his belly.
Rohita heard of this,
and he went from the forest to the village.
Indra, approaching him in the form of a man, said:
"O Rohita, we have heard that prosperity belongs to one who is weary from various labors;
O Indra-like man, even a wicked person is a friend to one who travels."
"‘The red one indeed moves,’ said the Brahmin; ‘he indeed moves. Having said this, he wandered in the forest for a second year. Then he went from the forest to the village.
Indra, approaching him in the form of a man, said: "Bhaga sits for one who is sitting; Bhaga stands upright for one who stands;
Bhaga lies down for one who is reclining; Bhaga moves for one who moves."
"‘Move along, Rohita! Move along!’—thus indeed did the Brahmin speak to me.
He wandered in the forest for a third year.
Then he went from the forest to the village.
Indra, approaching him in the form of a man, said:
"The Kali age is the man lying down; when he is about to rise, he is the Dvāpara age;
having risen, he is the Tretā; and moving about, he becomes the Kṛta."
"‘Rohita, move on! Move on!’—thus a Brahmin spoke to him.
He wandered in the forest for a fourth year.
Then he went from the forest to the village.
Indra, approaching him in the form of a man, said:
"The two shins move about like flowering plants; the self, seeking to thrive, is the fruit-bearing tree.
All his evils lie prostrate, slain by fatigue upon the path."
"‘Rohita, move on indeed!’—‘A Brahmin has indeed told me so,’ he thought.
He wandered in the forest for a fifth year.
Then he went from the forest back to the village."
Indra, approaching him in the form of a man, said:
"Truly, one who wanders finds honey; one who wanders finds the ripe udumbara fruit.
Behold the ascetic of the sun, he who does not grow weary while wandering."
"‘Move along, Rohita,’ said the Brahmin; ‘move along indeed!
[Thinking thus,] he wandered in the forest for the sixth year.
He then went from the forest to the village."
Indra, approaching him in the form of a man, said:
"One who wanders finds honey; one who plucks finds the parūṣaka fruit.
One who rises up finds prosperity; one who sits down preserves nothing at all."
"‘One must indeed wander as Rohita,’ so said the Brāhmaṇa to me: ‘One must indeed wander.
Thus he wandered in the forest for a seventh year. He then approached the seer Ajīgarta Sauyavasa in the forest, who was about to eat his own son, being overcome by hunger.
He had three sons: Śunahpuccha, Śunaḥśepa, and Śunolāṅgūla. He said to him, "O Seer, come now; I shall redeem myself by means of one of these [sons]. I will give you a hundred cows."
Restraining his eldest son, he said, "Is this not he? "Certainly not, this is not he," replied the mother to her youngest son.
They two agreed upon Śunaḥśepa as the middle one.
Having given him a hundred [cows], he took him and went from the forest to the village. Having approached his father, he said:
"Come now, I shall redeem myself by means of this," he said.
Having replied, "So be it," he addressed King Varuṇa:
"I shall sacrifice to you with this."
"So be it," he replied. "A Brāhmaṇa is indeed superior to a Kṣatriya.
It was for him that [the sage] proclaimed this royal consecration sacrifice (*rājasūya-yajñakratu*).
He sacrificed this person as the victim at the Rājasūya.
Viśvāmitra was his Hotṛ,
Jamadagni the Udgātṛ, Jamadagni the Adhvaryu, and Vasiṣṭha the Brahman.
Therefore, when [the victim] had been brought forward, they could not find anyone to immolate him.
Then Ajīgarta Sauyavasi said:
"Give me another hundred [cows], and I will immolate him."
They gave him another hundred;
he yoked it for him.
But for that animal which had been brought forward, yoked, and carried around with fire, they could not find a person to spread the grass.
Ajīgarta Sauyavasi said,
"Give me another hundred, and I will deliver him.
They gave him another hundred.
He went forth at night with his sword unsheathed.
Then Śunaḥśepa looked about and thought, "They will surely enter me as if I were non-human; come, let me take refuge with the deities."
He first approached Prajāpati among the deities with this Ṛgvedic verse: "To whom now, to which of the immortals?
Prajāpati said to him:
"You are indeed closest to Agni; go to him."
He approached Agni with this verse: "Of Agni, the first of the immortals...
Agni said to him:
"Savitar indeed rules over instigations; go to him alone."
He approached Savitṛ with this triplet beginning, "O God Savitṛ, toward you... (RV 6.71.1–3).
Savitṛ said to him:
"You have indeed been appointed for King Varuṇa; go to him."
Savitar said:
"You have been appointed to King Varuṇa;
go to him. He approached King Varuṇa with the thirty-one verses that follow.
Varuṇa said to him:
"Agni is indeed the mouth of the gods and their heart; praise him, and then I shall release you. He praised Agni with the following twenty-two verses.
Agni said to him:
"Praise all the gods, and then I shall release you.
He praised all the gods with this verse: "Homage to the great ones, homage to the small ones."
All the gods said to him:
"Praise Indra now, and then we shall release you.
He praised Indra with this hymn, beginning with "For whether [thou art], O true Soma-drinker," using fifteen verses from the latter [hymn].
Therefore, Indra, being praised, gave him a golden chariot without thought.
He approached him with this verse beginning, "Ever, O Indra...
Indra said to him:
"Pray now to the Aśvins, and then I shall release you," [he said].
He then praised the Aśvins with the following triplet of verses. The Aśvins spoke to him:
"Pray now to Uṣas; then we shall release you.
He praised Uṣas with the following triplet of verses.
With each verse as it was recited, his bonds were further loosened, and the belly of the descendant of Ikṣvāku became smaller.
Whenever an excellent Ṛgvedic verse was recited, his fetters were loosened, and the descendant of Ikṣvāku became free from disease.
Then the officiating priests said to him,
"You alone must reach the conclusion of this day's ritual."
Then Śunaḥśepa beheld this direct pressing.

Having pressed [the Soma] with these four verses beginning, "For whatever [is found] in every house," he poured the residue into the wooden vat (droṇakalaśa) with the verse, "Bring [the residue] for the two lips."
Then, while [the sacrificer] was holding on to him, he offered oblations with the first four verses of this very hymn.
Then he led him down to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) with these two ṛg-verses: "O Agni, you are our nearest one... and "O Agni, you who know the way of Varuṇa...
Then he caused him to worship the fire with this verse: "Like Śunaḥśepa, who was bound for a thousand..."
Then Śunaḥśepa ran into the lap of Viśvāmitra.
Ajīgarta, the son of Suyavasa, said to him:
"Give me back my son."
"No," said Viśvāmitra,
"the gods indeed bestowed this upon me.
He was thus known as Devārāta Vaiśvāmitra.
Ajīgarta Sauyavasi said to him:
"Let us both call upon him. "So be it," he replied.
The seer of the Aṅgiras clan was known by birth as Ajīgarta Śrutakavi.
"O Seer, do not depart from the ancestral lineage; come back to me!
Thus [he spoke]. Then Śunaḥśepa said:
"They saw you with the sword in hand, for you did not wish to settle among the Śūdras."
"O Aṅgiras, you chose three hundred cows from me.
To him, Ajīgarta Sauyavasi said:
"My son, that sinful deed committed by me truly torments me."
"Therefore, I renounce it to you; let hundreds of cows be returned to me.
Thus he spoke. Then Śunaḥśepa said:
"He who would once commit an evil deed might commit another sin after that."
"Do not depart from the path of the Śūdras; you have committed an act that cannot be reconciled.
Thus he spoke. Viśvāmitra then explained: "Or rather, he said, 'It is irreconcilable. [The son replied:
"O Prince, speak in such a way that you may make us understand it as something formidable."
"Just as I am an Aṅgiras, may I enter into the state of being your son.
To him, Viśvāmitra said:
"May you be the eldest among my sons; may your offspring be the most excellent.
You shall receive my divine inheritance; for this reason, I invite you.
Thus he spoke, and Śunaḥśepa replied.

"O you who possess true discernment, speak out for my sake, out of friendship for me, and for my prosperity, so that I, O bull among the Bharatas, may attain the status of being your son. Thus [he spoke].
Then Viśvāmitra addressed his sons.
"Listen, O Madhucchandas, Ṛṣabha, Reṇu, Aṣṭaka, and whoever else are your brothers; stand firm for this seniority! Thus [he spoke].
He indeed had one hundred and one sons.
There were exactly fifty elder sons of Madhucchandas and fifty younger ones.
Those who were the elders did not consider it right;
he spoke out against them.
"May your offspring consume [the enemy] at the end.
These are they: the Andhras, the Puṇḍras, the Śabaras, and the Mūcīpas.
They cite the fact that the Udīcyas have many Dasyus, and that among the Dasyus, those of the Vaiśvāmitra lineage are the most numerous.
Then those who were younger, beginning with Madhucchandas, considered it well.
Madhucchandas sang:
"In that which our father has brought together, in that we stand."
"We shall all be before you; we are behind you.
Thus [they spoke]. Then Viśvāmitra, being gratified, praised his sons:
"O sons, you shall indeed be possessed of cattle and rich in progeny."
Those who, showing me favor, have made me possessed of heroes;
those singers who, with divine bounty as their leader, have made me rich in heroes—may all these sons be successful for me; this is your formal address.
O Kuśikas, this hero Devārata is yours; follow him! May you and your inheritance attain the knowledge which we know. All these Vaiśvāmitras, united and possessing equal wealth, have come together.
The Gāthins established themselves for the sake of Devārāta’s preeminence and supremacy;
the seer Devārāta studied both types of inheritance,
and the Gāthins were established in the lineage of the Jahnus and in the Veda of the gods.
This is the narrative of Śunaḥśepa, consisting of more than a hundred Ṛgvedic verses and being immeasurable.
He indeed recites it for one who has been consecrated;
he recites it while seated upon a golden cushion.
Seated upon a golden cushion, he receives [the recitation]:
"Om" is the response for a Ṛc verse;
likewise, "So be it" (tathā) is the response for a Gāthā.
"Om" indeed belongs to the divine, and "So be it" belongs to the human. By means of both the divine and the human, he completely releases him from all sin.
Therefore, whatever king may be victorious, even if he is not performing a sacrifice, he should have this narrative of Śunaḥśepa recited.
Indeed, not even the slightest trace of sin remains in this [place].
A thousand [cows] are for the one who recites, a hundred for the one who responds, and these two [hundred] are for the seats.
Even those desiring sons cause themselves to be recited [to].
"They obtain sons, indeed; they obtain sons.
Prajāpati desired:
"May I attain all desires; may I pervade all expanses."

He beheld this three-night sacrificial rite, the Aśvamedha; he took it up. He sacrificed with it. Having sacrificed with it, he attained all desires and achieved all prosperities. In the same way, when the sacrificer sacrifices with the Aśvamedha, he attains all desires and achieves all prosperities.
ŚŚS 16.1.2: He offers to the great officiants four vessels: handfuls, cupped palms, and open hands.
ŚŚS 16.1.3: It is of twelve kinds. ŚŚS 16.1.4: For the year indeed consists of twelve months.

ŚŚS 16.1.8: He should lie down without drawing his thighs together.

Then he offers a cake on eight potsherds for Agni.
Indeed, Agni is the mouth of the gods; thus he gratifies the gods from their very mouth. Then he offers a pap for Pūṣan, the maker of paths.
Pūṣan is indeed the lord of paths;
thus he provides a safe journey for the horse.
They release a horse of every form, endowed with speed, for the sake of the year, fulfilling all desires except for unchastity.

ŚŚS 16.1.16: One hundred armored princes of the royal lineage, armed with quivers; the sons of charioteers and village chiefs, wearing sacred threads; and the sons of the kṣatriya charioteers—carrying staves and not letting [the horse] go astray—they guard the horse.

"May Savitṛ, the impeller, impel this sacrifice for me.

"He who is the god Savitṛ, the possessor of all treasures, let him come to all these created beings. "O god Savitṛ, [grant] all things; that god Savitṛ is indeed ours; [we belong to] the All-god, never to be surpassed."
ŚŚS 16.1.22: And the Hotṛ recites the *pāriplava* (the revolving narrative).

ŚŚS 16.2.26: "Its branches are the people; they sit here"—with these words, he instructs the students (*vayas*).
ŚŚS 16.2.27: "'The ancient Veda is this Veda'—thus he should recite the *Purāṇa*.
ŚŚS 16.2.28: "'Dharma-Indra'—this is for the tenth [day]."

ŚŚS 16.2.34: He recites all the Vedas.

ŚŚS 16.3.1: There are twenty-one sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), each twenty-one cubits (*aratni*) in height.

For he who shines yonder is indeed the twenty-one-fold one.
Thus he causes it to prosper in its own form.
From this, the horse was fashioned.

"From the sun, O Vasus, you fashioned the horse.
(ŚŚS 16.3.13) The horse, the gayal, the goat, and the castrated ram—these belong to Prajāpati.

"He who devours the life of women. Thus [it is said]. ŚŚS 16.3.37: No one at all reviles him.

[This occurs] during the theological debate (*brahmavādya*) in the assembly (*sadas*). ŚŚS 16.4.7.
The Hotṛ asks the Adhvaryu;
he replies with the second [verse];
the Hotṛ asks with the third.
With the fourth [verse], he replies:
"What light indeed is equal to the sun? What lake is equal to the ocean? What indeed is greater than the earth? Of what is there no measure? (ŚŚS 16.5.1)
The light is equal to Brahman and the sun; the lake is equal to the sky and the ocean.
Indra is greater than the earth, yet there is no measure for a cow.
Who indeed wanders alone? And who, indeed, is born again?
What indeed is the remedy for the cold? What indeed is the great receptacle?
The sun moves alone; the moon is born again.
Fire is the remedy for the cold; the earth is the great receptacle.
The Brahman priest asks the Udgātṛ.
The latter replies with the second [verse].
The Brahman asks with the third.
With the fourth [verse], he replies:
"I ask you, O friend of the gods, for the sake of wisdom: have you, with your mind, reached those places? In which three steps is Viṣṇu desired, and in which has he entered the entire world?"

ŚŚS 16.6.2: I am in those three steps in which the entire world has entered. In an instant, with a single limb, I encompass the earth and the sky, even the back of this heaven. ŚŚS 16.6.3: Into which [parts] has the Person entered? What things are fixed within the Person?
"O Brahmin, you have indeed spoken this riddle; what then will you answer us here?
"A man has entered within the five; they are fixed within that man. "Recalling this for you here, I respond: you do not surpass me through mere trickery."

"He has indeed conceived the seasonal germ, from which the sovereign was born"—

for the deities follow after Prajāpati, and thus he gratifies them each according to their proper place.

or that of the Viśvedevas"—
thus said Indrota Śaunaka— "'why indeed should they hasten? ŚŚS 16.7.5–7.

One should transpose the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* of the latter *mahiman* cup.

the Aśvamedha is everything.
"May I attain everything in its entirety.

that makes one thousand.

the Aśvamedha is everything.

it is for the sake of stability.
