ŚŚS 16.9.7: "The descendants of Parikṣit, performing the Aśvamedha sacrifices in succession, abandoned their evil karma through meritorious action. Thus it is said.
ŚŚS 16.9.8: By means of that [sacrifice], Ṛṣabha Yājñatura performed the Abhijit sacrifice.
Furthermore, this sacrificial verse (*yajñagāthā*) is also sung:
"In former times, when King Yājñatura sacrificed with a bull and a horse, Indra became intoxicated with Soma, and the Brahmins with their desired wealth. Thus it is said.
ŚŚS 16.9.11: With that [sacrifice], Parāhṇāra Vaideha performed the Viśvajit.
ŚŚS 16.9.12: Regarding this, this sacrificial verse (yajñagāthā) is also sung: ŚŚS 16.9.13: "On that day, they bound the sacrificial horse of Parāhṇāra."
"Hiraṇyanābha, the Kausalya, bestowed the quarters of the world in their fullness.
Thus [it is said]. ŚŚS 16.9.14: There was a Mahāvrata Atirātra sacrifice; with it, Marutta Āvikṣita performed the sacrifice.
ŚŚS 16.9.15: And regarding this, this sacrificial verse (yajñagāthā) is also sung:
"The Maruts dwelt as attendants in the house of Marutta;
Agni was the steward of Āvikṣita, and the Viśvedevas were the members of the assembly. Thus [it is said].
Thereupon, those deities indeed became his members of the assembly.
ŚŚS 16.9.18: The eastern direction belongs to the Hotṛ. ŚŚS 16.9.19: The southern direction belongs to the Brahman. ŚŚS 16.9.20: The western direction belongs to the Adhvaryu.
ŚŚS 16.9.21: [The wealth] of the Udgātṛ from the north.
ŚŚS 16.9.22: Whatever else belongs to non-Brāhmaṇas, other than land and men.
ŚŚS 16.9.23: In this very place [is the share] of the Hotrakas.
ŚŚS 16.9.24: But one should sacrifice in the middle.
ŚŚS 16.9.25: The sacrificial post (yūpa) has five animals as its branches. ŚŚS 16.9.26: The seasonal animals are sacrificed for a year.
ŚŚS 16.9.27: In spring, there are six [sacrifices] dedicated to Agni; ŚŚS 16.9.28: in summer, those dedicated to Indra;
ŚŚS 16.9.29: in the rainy season, those dedicated to the Maruts or to Parjanya.
In autumn, [the offerings] belong to Mitra and Varuṇa;
in winter, they belong to Bṛhaspati;
in the cool season, they belong to Indra and Viṣṇu.
Prajāpati, having sacrificed with the Aśvamedha, beheld the Puruṣamedha.
Whatever he had not obtained through the Aśvamedha, all that he obtained through the Puruṣamedha.
In the same way, when the sacrificer sacrifices with the Puruṣamedha, whatever he has not obtained through the Aśvamedha, all that he obtains through the Puruṣamedha.
ŚŚS 16.10.2: Everything [is] pertaining to the Aśvamedha. ŚŚS 16.10.3: And there is an addition. ŚŚS 16.10.4: Now, the oblations are for Agni Kāma, Dātṛ, and Pathikṛt.
Agni is indeed desire, the lord of the gods;
[this is] for the gratification of all the gods.
Agni is indeed the giver; he alone bestows the sacrifice upon him.
Agni is indeed the path-maker; he alone leads him back onto the path of sacrifice.
Having purchased a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya for a thousand [cows] and a hundred horses, they release him for a year, granting him all desires except for celibacy.
And in that very manner, they protect him.

ŚŚS 16.10.11: Then, for one year, there are oblations to Anumati, Pathyā Svasti, and Aditi. ŚŚS 16.10.12: [The rites] with the Sāvitra formulas are performed in reverse order. ŚŚS 16.10.13: The Nārāśaṃsa verses are recited according to the Pāriplava cycle.
"Permitted by Anumati, may you sacrifice with this sacrifice," he says.
Vāc is indeed Pathyā Svasti; thus he provides a safe journey for the sacrificer at the sacrifice.
Aditi is this [earth], and Aditi is the foundation; they thus establish him finally upon her, the undecaying one.
ŚŚS 16.11.1: The *śaunahśepa* hymns come first.
ŚŚS 16.11.2: Just as Śunaḥśepa, the son of Ajīgarta, was released when bound to the sacrificial post;
ŚŚS 16.11.3: so one should recite the first hymn.
ŚŚS 16.11.4: The second [stotra] is the Kākṣīvata.
ŚŚS 16.11.5: Just as Kakṣīvat Auśija won booty for Svanaya Bhāvayavya;
ŚŚS 16.11.6: and he should recite this at the end of the hymn.
ŚŚS 16.11.7: The third [sūkta] is that of Śyāvāśva.
ŚŚS 16.11.8: [The verse] beginning "As Śyāvāśva Ārcanānas Vaidadaśvi won gain...
ŚŚS 16.11.9: And the hymn beginning "Who are you, O men? (ke ṣṭhā naraḥ).
The fourth [stotra] belongs to Bhāradvāja. As Bharadvāja won the prize for Bṛbu, Takṣṇi, and Prastoka Sārñjaya, there are four verses beginning with "adhi bṛbuḥ prastoka."
The fifth [section] belongs to Vasiṣṭha.
Just as Vasiṣṭha became the domestic priest of Sudās Paijavana,
so too is the hymn beginning with "Two [sons] of the grandson" [to be recited].
The sixth [laud] is that of Medhātithi.
As for Plāyogi Āsaṅga, who being a woman became a man;
and the hymn beginning with "Praise, praise! (stuhi stuhi).
ŚŚS 16.11.19: The seventh [section] belongs to Vātsya. ŚŚS 16.11.20:
"Just as Vatsa Kāṇva won the prize at Tirindira Pāraśavya...
ŚŚS 16.11.21: And the hymn beginning with "A hundred times, O Tirindira... [is to be recited].
ŚŚS 16.11.22: [The hymn] beginning with *vāśam aṣṭamam*.
ŚŚS 16.11.23: [The verse] beginning with *yathā vaśo aśvyaḥ pṛthuśravasi kānīte sanim sasāna*. ŚŚS 16.11.24: And the hymn beginning with *ā sa etu ya īvad ā*.
ŚŚS 16.11.25: The ninth [sūkta] is that of Praskaṇva.
ŚŚS 16.11.26: Just as Praskaṇva won the prize at the sacrifice for Pṛṣadhra, Medhya, and Mātariśvan;
ŚŚS 16.11.27: And also the two hymns beginning with "Much indeed [is the power] of Indra."
The *nābhānediṣṭha* hymn is the tenth;
[the verse] "Just as the Mānava Nābhānediṣṭha, a descendant of Aṅgiras, won a good gain," and the hymn beginning with "Those who by sacrifice... [are also included].
The *nārāśaṃsa* verses are used;
for the *nārāśaṃsa* is indeed man.
Thus, he causes him to prosper by means of his own form.
There are twenty-five sacrificial posts (yūpas).
They are twenty-five cubits (aratnis) in length.
Ten are made of Bilva wood; twelve are made of Khadira wood.
The two posts near the entrance are made of *pitu-dru* wood;
the post standing at the fire-altar (*agniṣṭha*) is made of *rājjudāla* or *sārala* wood;
there are twenty-five sacrificial stakes for Agni and Soma.
Their performance is the same.
For the first and the last of the *aśvamedha* pressings, [the *stoma* is the twenty-onefold];
for the second, the *stoma* is the twenty-fivefold.
The person indeed consists of twenty-five [parts]. Thus, he causes him to prosper in his own form. The man, the gayal, the goat, and the hornless ram—these belong to Prajāpati.
The *gauro*, *gavaya*, *śarabha*, *uṣṭra*, *māyu*, and *kimpuruṣa* are the animals for the funeral pyre (*anustaraṇāḥ*).
There are twenty-five domestic animals for each of the twenty-five deities of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
Indeed, all these deities are the deities of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
ŚŚS 16.12.16: For the gratification of all the deities.
ŚŚS 16.12.17: Having caused the adorned man to smell the sacrificial vessel, [he recites] the eleven verses beginning with "udīratām avare," excluding the *praṇava*.
ŚŚS 16.12.18: "Agni is death" constitutes the *āprī* verses.
ŚŚS 16.12.19: He [recites] "mā enam agne... in the same manner during the *adhrigu* litany.
ŚŚS 16.12.20: Then they spread out for the man a garment made of *kauśa*, *tārpya*, *āruṇa*, and *āṃśava* fibers.
ŚŚS 16.12.21: The *udgātṛ* priest stands over the animal once it has been immolated with the *yāma* *sāman*.

ŚŚS 16.13.1: The Hotṛ priest is Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa. ŚŚS 16.13.2: Then the officiating priests (ṛtvij) attend upon him with two verses each, beginning with "pareyivāṃsam"; [the priests are] the Hotṛ, the Brahman, the Udgātṛ, and the Adhvaryu.
ŚŚS 16.13.3: From this they heal the sacrificer.

ŚŚS 16.13.4: "And, O gods, I release you who have been held fast; with an oblation, for the sake of life. May the wind blow medicine from your eyes, from your nostrils. With these verses, he proceeds in the proper order. ŚŚS 16.13.5: With the verse beginning "May life be extended," he performs the rites for the Nairṛta offerings, one by one. ŚŚS 16.13.6: He performs the rites for the Śaṃtāti offerings with three verses each.
ŚŚS 16.13.7: They cause the consecrated buffalo-cow to fall upon him.
ŚŚS 16.13.8: Both of them cover themselves completely with a head-covering.
ŚŚS 16.13.9: In that very manner, the sacrificer addresses them with mocking words.
ŚŚS 16.13.10: [The women] who revile him with the verses beginning, "The discarded woman, the one who does not drink, he whose eyes are unanointed, he who does not enjoy her whose hair is shaggy...
ŚŚS 16.13.11: With each subsequent verse, they respond by reviling him in turn.
ŚŚS 16.13.12: The Adhvaryu responds with the first verse.
"Arise, O noble lady; arise from here as the wife of a husband; arise from here, O Viśvāvasu!"—with these [verses] beginning with "aśmanvatī," they cause her to rise.
With the three verses beginning with "O Asunīti, lead our mind [back]," and "as for your [path] to Yama, like a yoke," he consecrates [her].
The Brahman priest causes [the bridegroom] to recite [these verses].
ŚŚS 16.13.16: There is a theological discussion (*brahmavādya*) among those seated at the assembly.
ŚŚS 16.13.17: The Hotṛ asks the Adhvaryu, "The cows [eat] the barley.
He replies with the second [verse].
With the third [verse] he asks;
with the fourth he replies.
"I have heard two paths of the fathers"—with these words, the Brahman priest asks the Udgātṛ.
He answers with the second [verse].
He asks with the one separated by one [verse]. He answers with the next [verse].
ŚŚS 16.14.1: [The verses] belonging to the Aśvamedha are from the Ājya[-stotra].
ŚŚS 16.14.2: One should recite both the [verses] belonging to the one-day rite (*aikāhika*) and those belonging to the Mahāvrata in the Ājya[-stotra].
ŚŚS 16.14.3: This is for the attainment of whatever desire exists in both the one-day rite and the Mahāvrata Ājya[-stotra].
ŚŚS 16.14.4: One should recite both the *prauga* hymns—the one belonging to the one-day rite (*aikāhika*) and the one belonging to the *mahāvrata*.
ŚŚS 16.14.5: Whatever desire is associated with the *prauga* hymn of the one-day rite and the *prauga* hymn of the *mahāvrata*, it is for the attainment of both of them.
ŚŚS 16.14.6: The midday pressing belongs to the *mahāvrata*.
The Rājanam is the back.
This Sāman, the Rājanam, is indeed shaped like a person;
thus, it endows him with his own Sāman.
The third pressing begins with the *anucara* verses from the sixth day onwards.
Indeed, the sixth day is characterized by the *nārāśaṃsa* verses.
Man, indeed, is the *nārāśaṃsa*.
Thus, it causes him to prosper in his own form.
The Mahādivākīrtya becomes the Agniṣṭoma-sāman.
Indeed, this Mahādivākīrtya is the Sāman that is anthropomorphic.
Thus he causes him to prosper by means of his own *sāman*.
It concludes with the *ṣoḍaśin* [stotra].
For man consists of sixteen parts.
Thus he causes him to prosper in his own form.
The fifth day of the *pṛṣṭhya* [six-day period] is the fourth day;
together with it, a man is given away.
ŚŚS 16.14.19: The sacrificial post has ten animals tied to its branches.
ŚŚS 16.14.20: There are twelve animals for each of the seasons.
ŚŚS 16.15.1a: Brahmā, being self-existent, performed austerities.
Having performed that austerity, he reflected:

"In austerity, indeed, there is no infinity; come, let me offer myself as a sacrifice into all beings. Having offered himself into all beings, he then offered all beings into the universal sacrifice (*sarvamedha*).
Thereupon, he indeed attained preeminence, sovereignty, and lordship over all beings.

In the very same way, when the sacrificer performs the Sarvamedha sacrifice, having offered himself as an oblation among all beings, he causes all beings to offer him as an oblation in the Sarvamedha.
Thereupon, he indeed attains preeminence, sovereignty, and lordship over all beings.
ŚŚS 16.15.2: The ritual action pertaining to the Puruṣamedha takes place first.
ŚŚS 16.15.3: They immolate a horse during the Agniṣṭut, Indrastut, Vaiśvadevastut, and Sūryastut [sacrifices].
ŚŚS 16.15.4: The fifth day is that of the Pauruṣamedhika.
There they immolate a human being;
the Vājapeya is the sixth [sacrifice],
and the Āptoryāma is the seventh.

There, they immolate all sacrificial animals, whatever living creatures there may be. They offer the omenta of those that have omenta; [they offer] the skins of those from which the omentum has been removed.

On the eighth and ninth days, which are the Triṇava and Trayastriṃśa stomas, they scatter the cuttings of herbs and trees. The final day is the Viśvajit, an Atirātra sacrifice characterized by all the Stomas and all the Pṛṣṭhas.
The Viśvajit is indeed everything: it has all the *stomas*, all the *pṛṣṭhas*, and its final day is the *atirātra*.
The Viśvajit is indeed everything: it has all the *stomas*, all the *pṛṣṭhas*, and it is an *atirātra*.
Everything is the Sarvamedha.
"May I attain everything in its entirety.
The sacrificial post has twenty animals and two branches.
There are twenty-four seasonal animals for each of the seasons.
ŚŚS 16.15.19: Here the Sarvamedha comes to a conclusion.
ŚŚS 16.15.20: The ground is given away together [with the other gifts].
ŚŚS 16.16.1: Having cast the lower fire-drill (araṇi) into the Gārhapatya fire.
Having consigned the Āhavanīya fire into the northern churning-stick (araṇi) and having internalized the fires within himself,
he should go forth into the forest.
Viśvakarman Bhauvana performed a sacrifice at its conclusion.
To him, Bhūmi said:
"No mortal whatsoever is worthy to give me away; O Viśvakarman Bhauvana, you intend to give me away."
"I shall submerge myself in the midst of the waters; your promise to Kaśyapa has been in vain. Thus she spoke.
Kaśyapa drew her out.

At the Vājapeya sacrifice, the Brahman priest mounts a cart-wheel made of Udumbara wood, [saying]: "By the impulse of Vāja, by the impulse of Savitṛ, may I ascend the highest firmament of Bṛhaspati, whose impulse is true."
ŚŚS 16.17.2: [The Sāman is] "of Indra" when a Kṣatriya is the sacrificer;
ŚŚS 16.17.3: "of the Maruts" when a Vaiśya [is the sacrificer].
ŚŚS 16.17.4: Having sat down upon that [spot], while the chariot wheels are fixed, he sings the Sāman three times without being prompted by a formal call (saṃpraisha).
Moreover, one should mutter three times:
"The young men have come forth for the prize; the prize-winners have arrived.
At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, may the coursers win the heavenly realms," and so on.
He descends with that same mantra.
In the descent, "I have descended" is the modification.
Having consumed the breath-consumption of the honey-cup from the golden vessel, he takes hold of the vessel.
"‘This sacrificer ascends to heaven; this sacrificer ascends to the celestial realm,’ [he says]. Or [they say]:
“They cause the sacrificer, as he climbs the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), to be touched with handfuls of salt.
In the *Rājasūya*, the consecrated sacrificer addresses the Brahman priest five times, saying: “O Brahman!”
In every case, he responds, "Thou art Brahman.
At the first [response], he says, "Thou art Savitṛ, the impeller.
At the second, he says, "Thou art Indra, possessing all power."
On the third [day], "Thou art Varuṇa, the lord of dharma";
on the fourth, "Thou art Rudra, the very gracious";
on the fifth, simply "Thou art Brahman."
ŚŚS 16.18.8: With his mind, he gives him two golden revolving discs.
ŚŚS 16.18.9: He accepts them with his mind.
ŚŚS 16.18.10: The officiating priests of the Aśvamedha, holding the reins, bathe the horse at two confluences of rivers.

ŚŚS 16.18.11: With this [verse], "May this king, having sacrificed with this sacrificial horse, be victorious; may he conquer those who are not devoted to the Brahmins," [the horse is released]. ŚŚS 16.18.12: And if they should touch him on the back while he is being sacrificed, he should mutter the formula, "I and you.
ŚŚS 16.18.13: When the middle day has concluded, they construct palaces in the various directions around the Āhavanīya fire.
ŚŚS 16.18.14: They strike them from above with enclosures provided with snares.
ŚŚS 16.18.15: During the night, the officiating priests offer oblations of all kinds of herbs.
ŚŚS 16.18.16: At the time of the morning recitation (prātar-anuvāka), they descend.
The attendants mount [the chariot].
They offer oblations until sunrise.
At this point, having purchased an Ātreya for a thousand [coins]—one who is fair-complexioned, tawny-eyed, wrinkled, covered in freckles, deformed, and impotent.
Having seized that woman by her hair, they lead her away.

Then, having caused him to enter the water, when the water flows over his face, the Adhvaryu offers an oblation upon his head with the formula: "To the horse-sacrifice, svāhā! To the murder of an embryo, svāhā!
Then they drive him out.
ŚŚS 16.18.21: "Their sins are cast off and they become free from debt.
ŚŚS 16.19.1: Now, therefore, follow the *ahīna* sacrifices that increase by one [day] each.
ŚŚS 16.19.2: What is of a single kind, that he obtains by means of a one-night sacrifice.
Now, that which is twofold is attained by means of the *dvirātra* sacrifice.
For there are two days and nights, two are heaven and earth, and these two are the supports.
Whatever is twofold—whether pertaining to the deities (*adhidaivata*) or to the self (*adhyātma*)—all that he obtains through this.
ŚŚS 16.20.3: An unmanifest collection of days should be extended to ten nights.
ŚŚS 16.20.4: There is a reduction from the beginning. ŚŚS 16.20.5: The final [day] takes the form of an Atirātra.
ŚŚS 16.20.6: There is a sacrificial fee every day.
ŚŚS 16.20.7: Those who have not been consecrated officiate for one who has been consecrated.
ŚŚS 16.20.8: The Ahīna sacrifices conclude with a month.
ŚŚS 16.20.9: In the event of a reduction in the *sutyā* days, they should increase the number of initiation (*dīkṣā*) days.
ŚŚS 16.20.10: One should not recite the *mahāvrata* for one who has not been initiated for a full year.
ŚŚS 16.20.11: Nor for one who has not maintained the fire-pot (*ukhā*) for a full year.
ŚŚS 16.20.13: This Agniṣṭoma is indeed the principal sacrifice and ritual. ŚŚS 16.20.14: [This is] for the sake of not diminishing the beginning of the sacrifice. ŚŚS 16.20.15:
But there are two *sampāta* verses at the insertion of the *nivid*.
ŚŚS 16.20.16: "tatam me yajñena vardhata" [is used] for the second [verse] in the Ārbhava- and Jātavedasīya[-śastra].
ŚŚS 16.20.17: And [it is used] at the Trirātra.
ŚŚS 16.20.18: [It is used] at the Abhijit, Viśvajit, Caturviṃśa, Mahāvratā, Go, or Āyus [sacrifices].

Whatever is twofold, that one obtains by means of the *dvirātra* sacrifice. Now, whatever is threefold, that one obtains by means of the *trirātra* sacrifice. For these worlds are three, the luminaries are three, and the sacrifice consists of three pressings (*tri-ṣavaṇa*).
Whatever threefold thing there is, pertaining to the deities or pertaining to the self, all that he obtains by means of this.
The three *stomas* beginning with the *trivṛt* belong to the first day;
those beginning with the *pañcadaśa* belong to the second.
ŚŚS 16.21.5: The *ājya* [laud] of the Brahman is sixteenfold.
ŚŚS 16.21.6: Those beginning with the twenty-onefold belong to the third day.
ŚŚS 16.21.7: The *agniṣṭoma* is the first day.
The Ukthya is the second;
the Atirātra is the third;
the Rathantara is the *pṛṣṭha* of the first.
The Vāmadevya-sāman is for the second [stotra];
the Bṛhat-sāman is for the third;
this world, indeed, is the Rathantara.
The intermediate world is the Vāmadevya;
yonder world is the Bṛhat.
This is for the attainment of these very worlds.
ŚŚS 16.21.17: From the *samūḷha*, the *ājya* [stotras] are drawn.
ŚŚS 16.21.18: From the middle *chandoma*, the *prauga* for the second day is in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
ŚŚS 16.21.19: "Aryamā" is the *marutvatīya* [śastra].
That which is the Marutvatīya hymn of the second day, he performs it on the third day.
He thereby makes these worlds possessors of enjoyment; therefore, indeed, these worlds enjoy one another.
Or, he may transpose the two days.
ŚŚS 16.21.23: *kas tam indra* is the *sāmapragātha* for the *niṣkevalya*.

ŚŚS 16.21.24: *mo ṣu tvā vāghataś cana* and [the following] are the two *pragāthas* serving as the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* for the Maitrāvaruṇa, with the exception of the two-footed verses (*dvipadā*).
ŚŚS 16.21.25: *kam navyaḥ* contains the word *ka*.
On the second day, regarding the hymns:
ŚŚS 16.21.27 states that for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, [the hymn] begins with "astāvi manma ubhayam śṛṇavat";
ŚŚS 16.21.28 states that the one containing the word *kad* begins with "kad ū nv asya".
ŚŚS 16.21.29: "śrāyanta iva sūryam śagdhy ū ṣu śacīpate" is for the Acchāvāka. ŚŚS 16.21.30:
"yad indra prāg apāg udak" contains the *kadvat* [verse].
ŚŚS 16.21.31: "kayā śubhīya" and "tad id āsīya" are the two *anividdhāna* [verses] for the second [turn].
The third pressing begins from the sixth [verse] starting with the *anucara*.
This indeed is the *sahasrastotrīya* by which Prajāpati sacrificed.
ŚŚS 16.22.2: This very [sacrifice] they call the Garga-trirātra.
ŚŚS 16.22.3: The second is the Aśvi-trirātra.
ŚŚS 16.22.4: On the middle day, they immolate a horse.
ŚŚS 16.22.5: The *Aghrigau* [stotras] are the *Aśvastomīya*.
ŚŚS 16.22.6: The third *Chandoma* is the *Pavamāna*. ŚŚS 16.22.7: The fourth is the *Parāka*.
ŚŚS 16.22.8: There are three *triṣṭoma* sacrifices with the *pṛṣṭhya-stomas*. ŚŚS 16.22.9: This indeed is the *parāka* sacrifice.
ŚŚS 16.22.10: One desiring to depart from this world should sacrifice with this.
ŚŚS 16.22.11: For one who desires a firm foundation, they say it is the *dvaiparāka*.
ŚŚS 16.22.12: For indeed, one *jagatī* consists of two *gāyatrīs*.
ŚŚS 16.22.13: This world is *gāyatra*; thus he finds a firm foundation in this world, in a state of stability from which there is no falling away.
The *jyotis*, *go*, and *āyus* [sacrifices] constitute the Kusuru-bindu three-night rite.
On the first day, he gives three hundred [cows],
and thirty-three with five parts (*kalā*).
In this manner, it is the second [cow], and in this manner, the third.
Then, only one-thousandth part of a cow remains;
having redeemed that with another cow, one should perform the rite.
"They say it should not be performed," they say, "for the sake of the sacrificer's prosperity.
"Whichever of those going [to the fire] should stop first, that one should be [the one who performs it]," they say;
for that is a sign of non-falling away.
Regarding those [women] who are standing together, they say that she who sits down first should be [the one chosen];
for they say this is the form for procreation.
They also say that she who is the most excellent should be [the one chosen].
ŚŚS 16.22.28: "I shall make [him] the best.

ŚŚS 16.22.29: At the *sarvavedas* three-night sacrifice, the Brahman priest is one who has performed the *triśukriya* rite and whose lineage on both sides extends for three generations of Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*).
ŚŚS 16.22.30: Whatever is threefold, that he attains through the three-night sacrifice.
Now, that which is fourfold is [attained] by means of the Catūrātra sacrifice;
for cattle are indeed fourfold,
and moreover, they are four-footed.
Whatever fourfold [knowledge] there is—whether concerning the deities (*adhidaivata*) or concerning the self (*adhyātma*)—all that he obtains by means of this.
The first day is the *trivṛt*, the second is the *pañcadaśa*, the third is the *saptadaśa*, and the fourth is the *ekaviṃśa*.
These four *stomas* are indeed sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) of diverse powers; therefore, for one who knows thus, four sons of diverse powers are born among his progeny.
ŚŚS 16.23.7: This indeed is the four-night sacrifice of Jamadagni. ŚŚS 16.23.8: Now follows the four-hero sacrifice of Atri.
ŚŚS 16.23.9: The morning pressing of the first day is the *trivṛt*, the midday pressing is the *pañcadaśa*, and the third pressing is the *saptadaśa*.

The morning pressing of the second day consists of the fifteen-versed stoma; the midday pressing is seventeen-versed; the third pressing is twenty-one-versed. The morning pressing of the third day is seventeen-versed; the midday pressing is twenty-one-versed; the third pressing is twenty-seven-versed.
The morning pressing of the fourth day is twenty-one-versed; the midday pressing is twenty-seven-versed; the third pressing is thirty-three-versed.
They proceed, omitting each stoma one by one and generating each one by one.
By means of that, four heroes of diverse prowess are born for him from the fore-offerings;
for the stoma is indeed a hero.
Its weapon is the Rathantara as the Pṛṣṭha-stotra for the first day;
the Niṣkevalya-śastra is the Sajaniya hymn.
ŚŚS 16.23.18: At the second *nivid*-insertion, [the stotras] are performed with the *kayā śubhīya*, the *tad id āsīya*, or [the *vā*].
ŚŚS 16.23.19: At the third [pressing], when the *vairūpa* is the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*, the third pressing is derived from the *vairāja*.
ŚŚS 16.23.20: At the fourth [pressing], when the *vairāja* is the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*, the third pressing is derived from the *vairūpa*.
Or it is the ordinary Atirātra;
they call that the Vaiśvānara.
The Abhijit is the fourth of the Ābhiplavika days.
The Viśvajit [sacrifice] is for others; or the Vaiśvānara or the Mahāvrata. Whatever fourfold [sacrificial rite] there is, that one obtains by means of the Catūrātra.
Now, that which is fivefold is accomplished by means of the Pañcarātra.

The *paṅkti* consists of five feet, and the sacrifice is indeed fivefold; therefore, whatever is fivefold—whether pertaining to the deities (*adhidaivata*) or pertaining to the self (*adhyātma*)—all that he obtains by this.
The first day is the *trivṛt*, the second is the *pañcadaśa*, the third is the *ekaviṃśa*, the fourth is the *saptadaśa*, and the final day is the *catuṣṭoma* *atirātra*.
This very [earth] is indeed in the form of these [waters];
this [earth] is in the form of the Trivṛt;
this [earth] is in the form of the Pañcadaśa.
This [is the stoma] of the twenty-one-fold;
this is of the seventeen-fold;
this is of the four-fold Atirātra.

Because the twenty-one-fold hymn-form (*ekaviṃśastoma*) is the most excellent among the *stomas*, therefore this [thumb] is the most excellent among these [fingers]. And because the four-fold hymn-form (*catuṣṭoma*) is the final day of the *atirātra* sacrifice, therefore this thumb reaches across all the fingers.
Its ritual recitation (*śastra*) is as follows.
The fourth [day] consists of three days of the *ābhiplavika* type.
For the fifth [day], there are two pressings; for the sixth, which is the *pṛṣṭhya*, the third pressing belongs to the fifth [day].
Or, there may be five *ābhiplavika* [days].
The third pressing occurs on the fifth day after the *uttama* (last) [day].
The *abhijit* is the fourth of the *ābhiplavika* days;
the *viśvajit* is for the others.
Either the Vaiśvānara or the Mahāvrata;
or for both [of these], the Abhijit is the fourth and the Viśvajit is the fifth. Whatever is fivefold, that one attains by means of the Pañcarātra sacrifice.
Now, that which is sixfold is attained by means of the six-night rite.
There are six seasons and six *stomas*; whatever is sixfold, whether pertaining to the deities (*adhidaivata*) or pertaining to the self (*adhyātma*), all that he obtains through this.
[The three-day period consists of] the *Abhijit*, the *Viśvajit*, and either the *Vaiśvānara* or the *Mahāvrata*.
ŚŚS 16.25.4: Or immediately following [the Abhijit], there is the Mahāvrata;
ŚŚS 16.25.5: the Viśvajit is the sixth [day];
ŚŚS 16.25.6: [this is] either the Pṛṣṭhya or the Abhiplava.
That which is sixfold, he obtains by means of the six-night rite;
then that which is sevenfold, he obtains by means of the seven-night rite.
There are seven vital breaths and seven meters; whatever there is that is sevenfold, whether pertaining to the deities or to the self, all that he obtains by this.
The three-day period consists of the Abhijit, the Viśvajit, the Mahāvrata, and the Vaiśvānara.
Now follows the intercalation of the year:
the standard Agniṣṭoma, the Caturviṃśa, the Abhijit, the Viṣuvat, the Viśvajit, the Mahāvrata, and the Vaiśvānara.
ŚŚS 16.26.6: This indeed is the seven-night sacrifice of the Seven Seers (Saptarṣis).
ŚŚS 16.26.7: They call this very one the Janaka Saptarātra.
ŚŚS 16.26.8: The Abhijit is the seventh of the Ābhiplavika [days].
The Viśvajit [sacrifice] belongs to the others; or the Vaiśvānara or the Mahāvrata. Whatever is sevenfold, that he attains by means of the Saptarātra.
Now, that which is eightfold is attained by means of the eight-night rite (*aṣṭarātra*).

There are eight Vasus; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables. Whatever is eightfold, whether with respect to the deities (*adhidaivata*) or with respect to the self (*adhyātma*), all that he obtains by this. The Abhijit is the seventh of the *ābhiplavika* days.
The Viśvajit is for the others;
or the Vaiśvānara or the Mahāvrata;
or for both, the Abhijit is the seventh and the Viśvajit is the eighth.
That which is eightfold, one obtains through the eight-night sacrifice. Now, that which is ninefold, one obtains through the nine-night sacrifice.

There are the four quarters, the four intermediate directions, the upward direction, and this [earth] as the ninth; the *bṛhatī* meter has nine syllables. Whatever there is that is ninefold, whether concerning the deities (*adhidaivata*) or concerning the self (*adhyātma*), all that one obtains by means of this.

The six-day period consists of the Abhijit and Viśvajit, followed by either the Vaiśvānara or the Mahāvrata; or else, immediately after the Abhijit comes the Mahāvrata, with the Viśvajit as the ninth day. The Jyotis Agniṣṭoma, the Gau Ukthya, and the Āyus Atirātra—these three they perform; this is called the *śalalīpiśaṅga*. Whatever is ninefold, that one attains through the nine-night sacrifice.

Now, that which is tenfold is attained by means of the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*). The *virāj* consists of ten syllables; it is the *vilāḷ*, the food. Whatever is tenfold, whether pertaining to the deities (*adhidaivata*) or pertaining to the self (*adhyātma*), all that he obtains by this. There is either the one-and-a-half-day *abhiplava* or nine *agniṣṭoma*s.
The Daśarātra is a modification of the *saṃsthā*s.
And there is also the Vaiśvānara [offering].
Having performed this sacrifice, Jala Jātūkarṇya attained the office of domestic priest for three kings: the Kāśyas, the Videhas, and the Kosalas.

Śvetaketu, having meditated upon his father’s prosperity, reproached him, thinking: "O gray-haired man, you have failed to provide me with the desire for sacrifice, or indeed to endow me with such prosperity and fame as this.
He said to him:
"Do not speak thus to me, my son. I had already understood the sacrifice as a mental rite (*yajña-kratu*); it was only that I wished to learn it in its entirety from a true Brahmin."
And indeed, it happened exactly as he had told him. This is the sacrifice for one who desires the office of domestic priest (*purodhā*). He who knows thus attains the office of domestic priest.
The recitation (śastra) for the Trikakuda sacrifice follows from the Samūḷha Catuṣṭoma;
then there is the Mahā-trikakuda,
and the Chandoma-trikakuda.
The Agniṣṭut, Indrastut, Vaiśvadevastut, Pṛṣṭhya, and Vaiśvānara;
the six-day period consisting of the Abhijit and Aśvajit, the Mahāvrata, and the Vaiśvānara;
and the standard Agniṣṭoma as the ninth, or the Viśvajit as the eighth, with [the Daśarātra] as the tenth.
Whatever is tenfold, that he obtains by means of the ten-night sacrifice. Now, whatever is elevenfold, that he obtains by means of the eleven-night sacrifice.

The *triṣṭubh* meter consists of eleven syllables, and cattle are of the nature of the *triṣṭubh*; therefore, whatever is elevenfold—whether pertaining to the deities (*adhidaivata*) or to the self (*adhyātma*)—all that he obtains by means of this.
The ten-night rite has its meters arranged in order;
the eleventh day is the Viśvajit;
they call that the Pauṇḍarīka.
The sacrificial fee is ten thousand [cows]. Some say that eleven hundred horses constitute the fee.
The twelve-day sacrifice has been described.
ŚŚS 16.30.12: These are *agniṣṭoma*s at the beginning and *atirātra*s at the end; they are successive, each one increasing by one, and constitute the *ahīna* sacrifices.
ŚŚS 16.30.13: He who knows thus attains that ever-increasing prosperity, the *virāj*, and the eating of food—yea, he who knows thus, yea, he who knows thus.
ŚŚS 17.1.1: Now, therefore, [the ritual] of the *mahāvratas*.
ŚŚS 17.1.2: A few days prior [to the sacrifice], the Hotṛ causes the swing-seat to be hewn from the Udumbara tree while it is still standing.
ŚŚS 17.1.3: While the tree is still standing.
ŚŚS 17.1.4: Before the rising of the sun.
If it is not found in the east, then perhaps in the north;
if in the south; or if it should be in the west.
Having cut it at the root, whether standing facing east or north, he should uproot it if it be a small *udumbara* tree.
Alternatively, they may join together three planks;
that [structure] is as long as an arm and faces east.
ŚŚS 17.1.11: It is one *aratni* in width.
ŚŚS 17.1.12: It is well-finished.
ŚŚS 17.1.13: Its tip is clearly marked.
ŚŚS 17.1.14: He causes it to be split into four parts at the ends.
ŚŚS 17.1.15: Then they cut off the two forked branches of this *udumbara* tree or another [tree]. ŚŚS 17.1.16:
At a distance of one man's length.
And a bamboo pole.
If a *udumbara* tree is not available, one should prepare this from whatever other fruit-bearing tree there may be that has an auspicious name.
Then, they have two ropes made of muñja grass prepared.
ŚŚS 17.2.2: It should be firm. ŚŚS 17.2.3: It should be threefold.
ŚŚS 17.2.4: It should be twice as long as the [other] two.
ŚŚS 17.2.5: This much [space] is on both sides of the Hotṛ.
ŚŚS 17.2.6: They prepare a throne-seat made of Udumbara wood for the Udgātṛ.
ŚŚS 17.2.7: Its legs are one span (prādeśa) in length.
ŚŚS 17.2.8: The head-boards and the side-pieces are a span (aratni) in measure.

ŚŚS 17.2.9: Having joined them together, they weave them with double-stranded cords made of muñja grass, which are smooth and stretched out straight. ŚŚS 17.3.1: Then they prepare this lute (*vīṇā*) with a hundred strings.
ŚŚS 17.3.2: Its *sūnā* (slaughtering post) is made of *pālāśa* wood.
ŚŚS 17.3.3: The staff is made of *udumbara* wood.
ŚŚS 17.3.4: Or alternatively, the *sūnā* may be made of *udumbara* wood and the staff of *pālāśa* wood.
ŚŚS 17.3.5: They sew it together on the outside with the hide of a bull, entirely red and with the hair facing outwards.
ŚŚS 17.3.6: At its base, they pierce the handle ten times.
ŚŚS 17.3.7: There, they fasten ten ropes each [to each hole].
ŚŚS 17.3.8: At the beginning, they tie them separately.
ŚŚS 17.3.9: A lute with a staff-handle and a hundred strings is prepared.
ŚŚS 17.3.10: A reed-flute with branches and leaves is prepared for playing.
ŚŚS 17.3.11: Or a reed that has bent by itself.
ŚŚS 17.3.12: The wives prepare a *ghāṭa*, a *karkarī*, *avaghaṭarikās*, *kāṇḍavīṇās*, and *piccorās*.
ŚŚS 17.3.13: One should play the *piccorā* with its mouth [of the instrument] facing upwards.
ŚŚS 17.3.14: By means of playing the *kāṇḍavīṇā*. ŚŚS 17.3.15: That [instrument] they call the *ghāṭarī*.
ŚŚS 17.3.16: If one plays the *ghāṭarī* softly, it should be the *sārāti*.
ŚŚS 17.3.17: He should cause his enemy to be born.
ŚŚS 17.4.1: The Adhvaryu prepares four drums with their fastenings.
ŚŚS 17.4.2: On both sides of the eastern door-post, at the junction outside the Sadas, he attaches two drums with their fastenings.
ŚŚS 17.4.3: On both sides of the door of the western [shed], at the junction of the interior of the *sadas* and the door-posts, he fastens two binding-ropes.
ŚŚS 17.4.4: If there are six [rope-strands], one is in the southern half of the *sadas* and one is in the northern half.
ŚŚS 17.4.5: They prepare a bundle of *muñja* and *kuśa* grass for the *adhvaryu*.
Standing upon that [seat], he responds.
Then the other initiated ones each prepare a grass mat (*bṛsī*) so that it shall be one span above the ground.
Now, for those women who are about to go around the *mārjālīya* shed, they prepare nine new jars for each of them.
ŚŚS 17.5.1: Then they prepare this horse-chariot with its protective fender extended.
ŚŚS 17.5.2: And a bow and thirty arrows.
ŚŚS 17.5.3: A king, or one of royal rank, who is a skilled archer.
ŚŚS 17.5.4: If neither a king nor one of royal rank should be found who knows this ritual procedure, he [the Adhvaryu] should perform it himself.
ŚŚS 17.5.5: To the north of the Āgnīdhra fire-shed, they erect two slanting, thick pillars facing east for the sake of digging out the pit (ākhaṇa).
ŚŚS 17.5.6: Over that, whether it be the *iḷasaṃvarta* or the *utkara* mound, they stretch a skin.
ŚŚS 17.5.7: One should pierce it through with a shaft provided with feathers.
ŚŚS 17.5.8: Behind the Āgnīdhra shed, outside the sacrificial altar, they dig a pit.
ŚŚS 17.5.9: They sew that [pit] up from the north with the hide of this bull to be immolated, with the neck pointing either eastward or northward and the hair facing upward.
At that time, they beat the earth-drum with the tail of that very [bull].
Then, they prepare a Śūdra and an Ārya, a woman and a man, and a eunuch and a bald man.
This is an ancient practice that has fallen into disuse; it should not be performed when these [other items] have been prepared.
ŚŚS 17.6.3: When the tenth day has concluded, they pile up the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds.
ŚŚS 17.6.4: [They also pile up] the *āgnīdhra* shed and the *patnīśāla*.
ŚŚS 17.6.5: Then they spread a thick layer with new *kuśa* grass.
ŚŚS 17.6.6: They set aside several bundles of *kuśa* grass for the morning seats (*bṛsī*).
ŚŚS 17.7.1: Then, during the latter part of the night, they commence the morning litany (*prātar-anuvāka*) for the Mahāvrata rite.
ŚŚS 17.7.2: He should recite it up to one thousand verses.
Its stoma is the twenty-fivefold;
the *pṛṣṭha* chant is the *rājana*;
the sacrifice is the *agniṣṭoma*.
ŚŚS 17.7.6: Now, these are the *pariṣṭavaṇīya* [stomas]: the *trivṛt*, the *pañcadaśa*, the *saptadaśa*, and the *ekaviṃśa*.
ŚŚS 17.7.7: Either the offering to Indra and Agni, or one from among the eleven [animal victims], is the *savanīya*.
ŚŚS 17.7.8: A bull for Indra and a goat for Prajāpati are to be immolated as additional offerings (*upālambhya*).
The *nirukta* [chant] belongs to Indra;
the *upāṃśu* [chant] belongs to Prajāpati.

When they proceed after the omenta have been offered, then, having washed this swing-mixed [implement] outside the altar, having entered by way of the path between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, and having carried it around the north of the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth, they place it in front of and to the north of the Hotṛ’s hearth, facing east, after having brought it into the *sadas* through the eastern door.

ŚŚS 17.7.12: In this very same way, whatever [vessels] are outside the sacrificial altar (*vedi*), having been brought back in such a manner as there is a path for movement during the creeping forward (*samprasarpaṇa*), they place them down to the north.
ŚŚS 17.7.13: Regarding that, the *Prātaḥsavana* (morning pressing) should be in the *Triṣṭubh* metre; this is the view of Paiṅgya, namely the *Śuṣkabhṛṅgārīya*. ŚŚS 17.8.1:
"To every clan, your guest..."—this is the *Ājya* (offering).

Having recited twelve [verses] by half-verses, he recites as an additional praise (*upasaṃśaṃsati*) the hymn "Agni the men kindle with their thoughts from the two fire-sticks" (*agnim naro dīdhitibhir araṇyoḥ*), consisting of twenty-five verses.
That is the prescribed recitation (*diṣṭa-śastra*).
The *praüga* is in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
ŚŚS 17.8.5: "kuvid aṅga namasā ye vṛdhāsaḥ" is for Vāyu and for Indra-Vāyu;
ŚŚS 17.8.6: and that for Mitra-Varuṇa is as at the Viṣuvat;
ŚŚS 17.8.7: "ka u śravat katamo yajñiyānām" is for the Aśvins.
ŚŚS 17.8.8: "kathā mahām avṛdhat kasya hotuḥ" is for Indra.
ŚŚS 17.8.10: "uta syā naḥ sarasvatī juṣāṇā" is for Sarasvatī. ŚŚS 17.8.11: That [offering] is arranged with three verses.
ŚŚS 17.8.12: His recitation is by quarters (pacchas).
ŚŚS 17.8.13: Or the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana) is that of the one-day rite (aikāhika).
ŚŚS 17.8.14: The morning pressing is thus established.
ŚŚS 17.9.1: Now, therefore, follows the midday pressing (mādhyaṃdina-savana).
ŚŚS 17.9.2: "As a chariot for aid, come to us... (*ā tvā rathaṃ yathā ūtaye*) is the introductory verse (*pratipad*) of the Marutvatīya [śastra].
ŚŚS 17.9.3: "O Vasu, this pressed soma-juice... (*idaṃ vaso sutaṃ andhaḥ*) is the following verse (*anucara*).

ŚŚS 17.9.4: This indeed is the continuous extension of the *nitya-ekāha*. ŚŚS 17.9.5: Having first recited the *vāsukra* hymn, "O singer, [the soma] has been pressed for me with impetuosity," he places the *nivid* in this *traiṣṭubha* hymn, "The great Indra, manly, who fills the people. ŚŚS 17.9.6: He should recite both hymns hemistich by hemistich.
Thus, indeed, is the Marutvatīya.
Now, therefore, follows the Niṣkevalya.
When the morning pressing has been completed, one should have two pits for the swing dug; such is the established rule.
"Regarding the *marutvatīya* [offering], it is auspicious," says Paiṅgya.

Having measured four finger-breadths behind his own *dhiṣṇya* hearth and its footprint, he places a plank there with its tip pointing north. Having placed two [stones] on both sides at a distance of four finger-breadths and having drawn two lines outside them at four finger-breadths [from the stones], he should have two pits for the swing dug—the southern one first, then the northern one.
They dig out [the earth] either towards the east or towards the north.
ŚŚS 17.10.6: Having fixed those two Viśākhas, he places the bamboo beam with its tip pointing northward.
ŚŚS 17.10.7: The Hotṛ measures it by means of his head.
ŚŚS 17.10.8: If it should be short, he measures it with his arms raised upward.
ŚŚS 17.10.9: When it has been firmly settled, he sprinkles it so that the two [ends] shall not be disturbed.
ŚŚS 17.10.10: Then he winds this plank of the swing four times at its ends with ropes so that it may not slip down.
ŚŚS 17.10.11: To the north of the southern swing-pillar, they tie the southern rope.

ŚŚS 17.10.12: To the south, they tie the northern cord to the northern pillar of the swing. ŚŚS 17.10.13: Having pressed it together, he throws it so that it remains at a distance of one span above the ground. ŚŚS 17.10.15:
He rubs it all around so that it is firmly fixed and does not wobble.
Having fastened it, he leans it against the northern post of the swing.
He should place it in its proper position when the *marutvatīya* śastra has been recited. Then the Adhvaryu, having taken up the draught for Mahendra, [proceeds] as follows.
He sits down facing east in front of the Hotṛ’s hearth (dhiṣṇya).
The Hotṛ says to him, "O Adhvaryu, come now and rest.

He goes out by the northern door, passing to the north of the northern post of the swing and to the north of the Adhvaryu; having entered the Āgnīdhra shed by the eastern door, he goes around the north of the Āgnīdhra hearth, sits down behind it facing east, bends his right knee, takes a portion from the vessel of clarified butter with the *sruva* spoon, and offers it as an oblation.

ŚŚS 17.12.1: "The *gāyatra* is long-lived; the *rathantara* is all-life; the *bṛhat-sāman* is total life; the *vāmadevya* is the life of life; the *yajñāyajñīya* is exceeding life. Through their life, may I become long-lived. For this [woman], may breath circulate for progeny and for the heart's delight. Having driven away all [obstacles] and having healed [all wounds], may there be a hundred autumns for me. *Svāhā!*"—with these words, he offers the first oblation. ŚŚS 17.12.1: "To heaven, *svāhā*; to the intermediate space, *svāhā*; to the earth, *svāhā*."—these are three [oblations]. ŚŚS 17.12.3: "To the cow, *svāhā*; to speech, *svāhā*; to the Lord of Speech (*vācaspati*), *svāhā*."—these are another three [oblations].
Whatever this is—*iti*, *haiti*, *ham*—let one utter it together with the divine. That we shall sacrifice for, which hastens toward us.
O King, we sacrifice to Speech; O Lord of Speech, be victorious for me!

Having offered the eighth oblation with the formula, "He who assails us—*svāhā*," and having placed the *sruva*-ladle in its proper place, he goes out by the way he entered. Standing in front of the *sadas* to the north of the *sruk*, facing east, he mutters the *parimāda* recitations:
"Speech! Life! All-life! All-life! Come hither! Even so, O Indra, come hither! Knowing all ways, O Maghavan, know [us]! (ŚŚS 17.12.5).
Then, standing right there, he worships Agni limb by limb:

with the words, "Homage to your Gāyatra; that which is your head, that which is your front," he worships the eastern half; with the words, "Homage to your Rathantara; that which is your right arm, that which is your right wing," he worships the right wing.
ŚŚS 17.13.3: "Homage to your great [form], that which is your upper arm, that which is your upper wing"—with these words, he touches the upper wing.
ŚŚS 17.13.4: "Homage to your Vāmadevya [form], that which is your middle, that which is your self"—with these words, he touches the middle.
ŚŚS 17.13.5: "Homage to your Yajñāyajñīya [form], that which is your tail, that which is your foundation"—with these words, he touches the tail.
ŚŚS 17.13.6: He should worship these portions [of the fire] while it is indeed kindled, if there is an *uttaravedi*.
ŚŚS 17.13.7: Then, standing right here, he worships the sun.
ŚŚS 17.13.8: "They should make the hall open to the sky," so say some.
ŚŚS 17.13.9: He worships with the [formula] beginning with "deśena.

ŚŚS 17.13.10: "Thou art Subhū, the best ray of the gods in their assembly; with that body wherewith thou quickenest the Brahman, quicken me therewith, procreate me therewith, protect me therewith; bestow upon me spiritual luster, food to eat, and brilliance; homage be unto thee; do not harm me. ŚŚS 17.13.11:
Then, turning to the right, he enters.
ŚŚS 17.13.12: Having sat down facing east on the swing behind [the altar], holding onto it or not letting go of it, he remains silent until the time of the creeping forward (adhisarpaṇa).
ŚŚS 17.14.1: He should cause the singers of the Sāmans (chandoga) to chant the three verses concerning the head from the front.
ŚŚS 17.14.2: He should exchange calls with the Adhvaryu priest from the front.

ŚŚS 17.14.3: Having recited twelve times in silence, he should respond; having instructed [the Prastotṛ] on the distributed [stotra], himself, and the word-connections (*padānuṣaṅga*), he should respond with the formula, "The *abhyavahṛta* has been recited.
ŚŚS 17.14.4: Then he says to the Prastotṛ, "When seven *stotriya* verses remain, announce it to us; for until then this [formula] is to be muttered.
ŚŚS 17.14.5: Then the Adhvaryu introduces the stotra.
At the very moment when the Udgātṛ ascends his throne, the Prastotṛ and the Pratihartṛ creep forward upon two mats,
as do the Upagātṛs. The Udgātṛ alone is the first to play the lute.
The wives follow him with shouts of approval;
they beat the drums;
they strike the earth-drum.
The makers of sound raise a clamor. Then, carrying full jars of water, they walk around the *mārjālīya* fire-altar three times, moving from right to left.

ŚŚS 17.14.16: Thereafter, [he moves] silently, turning to the right (prasaḷavi). ŚŚS 17.15.1: Then they yoke this horse-chariot. ŚŚS 17.15.2: [They do so] in front of the southern shoulder of the sacrificial altar (vedi).
ŚŚS 17.15.3: A king or one of royal rank, having put on his armor and taken up a bow and three arrows, mounts [the chariot].
ŚŚS 17.15.4: Moving three times around the altar from left to right, he pierces this earthen target.
ŚŚS 17.15.5: He should not pierce it through with a feathered arrow.
Thus a second time, thus a third time.
They loosen it toward the east and the north.
They release it right there.
ŚŚS 17.15.9: Then, when seven stotriya verses remain, the Prastotṛ [calls out] "The time for the *āhāva*.

ŚŚS 17.15.10: Then the Hotṛ, touching with his right forefinger both the plank of the swing and the ground, mutters: "May the Great One unite with the Great One. ŚŚS 17.15.11: Then, having placed his forefinger upon the upper plank of the swing, he mutters: "May the God unite with the Goddess."
ŚŚS 17.15.13: Then, holding the *prādeśa* at a distance of one *prādeśa* from the upper plank of the swing, he mutters: "May the Brahman be united with the Brāhmaṇī. ŚŚS 17.15.13:
Then, having placed the plank down, he anoints it three times and descends three times. ŚŚS 17.16.1:

Then, touching it with his chest and passing over its right side toward himself, he mutters: "Thou art the Arka; may the Vasus ascend thee by means of the Gāyatrī metre; may I ascend after them for the sake of sovereignty."
Then, crossing over the northern part of himself, he mutters: "May the Rudras ascend thee with the Triṣṭubh metre; may I ascend after them for self-sovereignty.
Then, crossing over the southern part of himself, he mutters: "May the Ādityas ascend thee with the Jagatī metre; may I ascend after them for universal sovereignty."
Then, while stepping over the northern part of himself, he mutters: "May all the gods ascend thee with the *anuṣṭubh* metre; I ascend after them, filled with desire.
Then, having composed himself and drawn down his two feet forward, he places them upon the ground. Then, having rubbed [the ground] three times, he breathes out three times.

ŚŚS 17.16.7: Then, having made a lap on the swing-board with the right side uppermost, he touches the rear of the swing-board with his right forefinger, saying: "May Prajāpati mount you; may Vāyu swing you. ŚŚS 17.16.8:
Then, having smelled [the board] three times and breathed upon it three times.
ŚŚS 17.16.9: Then, grasping his hands with the palms facing forward, he mutters:

ŚŚS 17.17.1: "May my speech be united with breath; may I be united with breath. May my eye be united with the mind; may I be united with the mind. May Prajāpati be united with the cattle; may I be united with the cattle. You are the fair-winged Garuḍa. I shall utter this speech which will accomplish much, desiring to accomplish much; it is that which seeks heaven through the arms, desiring to seek heaven. ŚŚS 17.17.2: Then, having anointed [himself] three times, he [performs] the downward inhalation three times. ŚŚS 17.17.3:
Having released his speech, he remains desiring to pour out the intoxicating drink (matsara), until the commencement of the chanting of the stotra.
ŚŚS 17.17.4: At the very moment the Hotṛ ascends the swing, everyone, including the householder, creep upon their grass mats.
ŚŚS 17.17.5: When the last stotriya verse remains, he unbinds the drums.
ŚŚS 17.17.6: He unbinds the earth-drum.
The makers of sound cease their noise.
Then, women carrying full jars of water circumambulate the *mārjālīya* shed.
Having poured out the jars upon the *mārjālīya* and set them down, they are released in the same manner as they were brought in.
"Here it is," he says.
Once this has been uttered, the Hotṛ restrains his speech until the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*. He follows the *upaprathāra* at the call for the *āhāva*.
He calls out after the *pratihāra*.
Having called out loudly, he makes the *him* sound three times in a whisper, then recites the *śastra* in a whisper and then silently.
Of that, of that—of that, of that.
Having called out loudly three times and having uttered the *him* sound silently, [he recites] these three verses:

"The Brahman was born first in the east," "This [earth] for the father, the royal one," and "May all the gods worthy of sacrifice hear me"—these are the *tūṣṇīṃ-śaṃsa*. He recites them silently, without the *praṇava*, verse by half-verse.
Then he releases his speech for himself.
"tad id āsa bhuvaneṣu jyeṣṭham" is the *stotriya* triplet (ŚŚS 18.1.4). This consists of nine verses (ŚŚS 18.1.5).
"vane na vā yo nyadhāyi cākann" consists of eight verses (ŚŚS 18.1.6).
ŚŚS 18.1.7: *śākmanā śokā aruṇaḥ suparṇaḥ*—this is a triplet (*tṛca*).
ŚŚS 18.1.8: *yo adadhāj jyotiṣi jyotir antar*, *mahat tan nāma guhyam puruspṛk*, and *idam ta ekam para ū ta ekam*—these three are the *ekapātini* verses.
ŚŚS 18.1.9: These [verses] amount to twenty-three.
ŚŚS 18.1.10: With the first [verse] recited three times, there are twenty-five [verses].
ŚŚS 18.1.11: This very self consists of twenty-five parts.
ŚŚS 18.1.12: He recites it accompanied by the *nada* (the roar).
ŚŚS 18.1.13: “nadam va odatīnām.
ŚŚS 18.1.14: The preceding words belong to the *triṣṭubh* meter; the subsequent ones belong to the *nada* [meter].
ŚŚS 18.1.15: Having joined the first word of the *nada* with the first word of the *triṣṭubh*, he pauses.
Having joined the second [verse] with the second *traiṣṭubha* [verse], he pronounces the *praṇava*.
Having joined the third [verse] with the third *traiṣṭubha* [verse], he pauses.
Having joined the fourth [verse] with the fourth *traiṣṭubha* [verse], he pronounces the *praṇava*.
ŚŚS 18.1.19: He recites the first [verse] thus expanded three times. ŚŚS 18.1.20:
The subsequent [verses] are recited in their regular order.
ŚŚS 18.1.21: Of that which is the third [verse] of the hymn, he omits its second half-verse as well as the second [half-verse] of the verse beginning with "nadasya."
He recites those two [verses] before the *dvipadās*.
Having recited the *ātman* [verse], he then recites the *sūdadohas*. He recites that [verse] beginning with "These are his *sūdadohas*" by half-verses.
ŚŚS 18.2.1: Then he recites these triplets pertaining to the head.

ŚŚS 18.2.2: "Indramid gāthinaḥ," "Indreṇa saṃ hi," "Indro dadhīcaḥ," "Ut tiṣṭhann ojasā saha," "Ud gha it abhi śrutām agham," and "Ud u tyam jātavedasam"—he should recite those triplets among these in which the Sāman-singers chant their hymns.
ŚŚS 18.2.3: Regarding the triplet "Ud u tyam jātavedasam," some indeed chant it as a group of nine verses.
If they should do so, he should recite this very [verse].
Regarding the verse "ud u tyam jātavedasam," some indeed chant it on the first *ṛc*.
If they should do so, he should bring forward those among the others whom he might desire.
Having recited those [verses] half-verse by half-verse, he then recites the *sūdadohas*.
Then he recites this triplet (*tṛca*) concerning the neck:
"He whose vigor here is crushing, whose impulse is joined with strength, whose power is overwhelming..."
Indra’s lofty and desirable [power], unassailable through its excellence; it is not to be assailed, nor has it ever been assailed. It is bold, courageous power.
"May he grant us that wealth which has a many-colored appearance;
O Indra, Lord of the Stoma, may this praise be among the people"—
having recited this verse by half-verses, one then recites the *sūdadohas*.
ŚŚS 18.4.1: “Lead us along the wide world, O Knower”—with these words [he recites] the *akṣa* verses.
ŚŚS 18.4.2: Having recited that [hymn] verse by verse, he then recites the *sūdadohas*.
ŚŚS 18.4.3: Then the *stotriya* of the *rathantara*, with repetition and forming the *kakubh* meter, and then the *sūdadohas*.

ŚŚS 18.4.4: Then [he recites] the *anurūpa* of the *rathantara*, with the *punarādāya* and the *kakup* formation; then the *sūdadohas*. ŚŚS 18.4.5: After that, having recited the *dhāyyā* verse by quarters, then the *sūdadohas*. ŚŚS 18.4.6: Then, having recited the *rāthantara pragātha* by half-verses, then the *sūdadohas*.

ŚŚS 18.4.7: The hymn beginning with *ya eka id davyaś carṣaṇīnām* is recited *pacchas*. Having omitted its second verse, one takes that which is the second verse of the following hymn (*viśvo hy anya ārir ā jagāma*) and makes it the second verse here. After reciting the hymn, one then recites the *sūdadohas* verse. ŚŚS 18.4.8: The triplet beginning with *tam indraṃ johavīmi maghavānam ugram* is the *prahastaka*. ŚŚS 18.4.9: Having recited that [triplet] *pacchas*, one then recites the *sūdadohas* verse.
ŚŚS 18.5.1: "Generating light with the sun, Indra, swift and like Aṅgiras, has come with this prayer;
the mighty one, invoked by hymns according to the Ṛta, has pierced the Dawn through the altar amidst the rivals. Thus [is the recitation] of the Akṣas. ŚŚS 18.5.2:
Having recited that [hymn] verse by verse, he then recites the Sūdadohas.

ŚŚS 18.5.3: Then [he recites] the stotriya of the Bṛhat[-sāman], with repetition and forming the *kakup* [verse]; then the *sūdadohas*. ŚŚS 18.5.4: Then the *anurūpa* of the Bṛhat[-sāman], with repetition and forming the *kakup* [verse]; then the *sūdadohas*. ŚŚS 18.5.5:
There is no *dhāyyā* here.
ŚŚS 18.5.6: Then, having recited the *bārhata* *pragātha* by half-verses, [he recites] the *sūdadohas*.

ŚŚS 18.5.7: The hymn beginning with "Every other enemy has departed" (*viśvo hy anya ārir ājagāma*) is recited by quarters (*padas*). Having omitted its second verse, he makes that which is the second verse of the hymn beginning with "He who alone is to be invoked by the peoples" (*ya eka id davyaś carṣaṇīnām*) its second verse here. ŚŚS 18.5.8: Having recited the hymn, [he recites] the *sūdadohas*.

ŚŚS 18.5.9: “viśvāḥ pṛtanā abhibhūtarṃ naram” is the triplet of the *prahastaka*. ŚŚS 18.5.10: Of this, he recites the first verse by quarters (*pacchaḥ*) and the two following verses by half-verses (*ardharcaśaḥ*). ŚŚS 18.5.11: Having recited the *prahastaka*, he then recites the *sūdadohas* verse.
ŚŚS 18.6.1: Then he recites these four-verse triplets (tṛcas).

ŚŚS 18.6.2: "For Indra, for the one who loves the pressed juice," "Indra, for the slaying of Vṛtra," "The singers of the Gāyatrī sing to you," and "Not for you, O great stones"—these are the four triplets.
ŚŚS 18.6.3: These [he recites] by half-verses (ardharcaśas).
"Thus indeed, O Soma, in this intoxication... (ŚŚS 18.6.4): this triplet is in the *paṅkti* meter; it is the *paṅkti-śaṃsa*.
"And many songs have come together unto thee, O Indra; then the Aṅgirases first assumed their vigor" (ŚŚS 18.6.5): these two triplets are in the *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* meters respectively.
Having recited them *pāda* by *pāda*, he then recites the *sūdadohas* verse.
ŚŚS 18.7.1: Then he recites these eighty [verses]. ŚŚS 18.7.2: He begins the Gāyatrī-aśīti with the verse, "Great is Indra, who by his might...
ŚŚS 18.7.3: These consist of fifteen triplets (ṛcas).
ŚŚS 18.7.4: "indra it somapā ekaḥ" and so on, eight [verses].
ŚŚS 18.7.5: "eva id eṣa tuvikūrmiḥ" and so on, three [verses].
ŚŚS 18.7.6: "ā ghā ye agnim indhate" and so on, fourteen [verses].
ŚŚS 18.7.7: Those are forty triplets.
ŚŚS 18.7.8: That is the first half-verse section (kapala). ŚŚS 18.7.9: Now follows the latter [half-verse section].
ŚŚS 18.7.10: The ten triplets beginning with *pra kṛtāny ṛjīṣiṇaḥ*.
ŚŚS 18.7.11: The five [verses] beginning with *apād u śipry andhasaḥ*.
ŚŚS 18.7.12: The four [verses] beginning with *ā tvā viśantv indavaḥ*.
ŚŚS 18.7.13: "yad adya kat ca vṛtrahan" and so forth, five [verses].
ŚŚS 18.7.14: "patnīvantaḥ sutā ime" and so forth, four [verses]. ŚŚS 18.7.15: "idam hy anv ojasā," "uttiṣṭhann ojasā saha," and "abhipra gopatim"—these are three triplets (tṛcas).
ŚŚS 18.7.16: Whatever has been performed by them previously, that one should remove.
ŚŚS 18.7.17: Or, if they should not perform it, one should indeed remove it.
ŚŚS 18.7.18: "He who brought [the gods] from afar" consists of ten triplets (ṛcas).
ŚŚS_18.7.19: Those are forty triplets (tṛca).
ŚŚS_18.7.20: After that is the Kapala.
ŚŚS_18.7.21: Then follow the Sūdadohas verses.
ŚŚS 18.8.1: One enters upon the Bārhata-aśīti with this [verse]: "O Indra, bring that which is for our enjoyment. ŚŚS 18.8.2: Those [verses] are nine direct *bṛhatī*s.
ŚŚS 18.8.3: There are three [verses] beginning with "All those heroic powers of yours, O Indra."
ŚŚS 18.8.4: "tam ghem itthā namasvinaḥ" and the following two [verses].
ŚŚS 18.8.5: "na sīm deva āpad" and the following six [verses].
ŚŚS 18.8.6: These twenty [verses] are manifest Bṛhatīs.
Now follow the *pragāthas*.
There are four [verses] beginning with "He who, truly, is the one who dwells among the people" (*yaḥ satrāhā vicarṣaṇiḥ*).
Having removed the four verses beginning with "Not even the priests indeed [should restrain you]" (*mo ṣu tvā vāghataś cana*), there is a *dvipadā* [verse].
ŚŚS 18.8.10: "ud id asya ricyate" consists of five [verses].
ŚŚS 18.8.11: "tat tvā yāmi suvīryam" and "yukṣvā hi vṛtrahantama" consist of two verses each.
ŚŚS 18.8.12: "yad indra prāk apāk udak" consists of seven [verses].
ŚŚS 18.8.13: "Pour forth, O possessor of many treasures"—these two [verses].
ŚŚS 18.8.14: "When the non-sage worshipped"—these five [verses].
ŚŚS 18.8.15: "He who is the powerful one, the bear, the horse"—these six [verses].
ŚŚS 18.8.16: Of these, he takes three.
ŚŚS 18.8.17: These are forty *pragāthas*.
ŚŚS 18.9.1: Then he recites the *bṛhatīs* that are directly perceived.
ŚŚS 18.9.2: "mahe cana tvām adrivaḥ" consists of twenty-five verses.
ŚŚS 18.9.3: Having recited twenty of them, one then recites the Sūdadohas verse.
ŚŚS 18.9.4: "ni gavyantaḥ" is the Nivid insertion verse.
Having recited that [verse] by the half-verse (*pacchas*), he calls for the *nivid* and inserts it.
Having recited that [verse] by the half-verse, separating it [from the next], he recites the hymn as a whole (*sama-sūktam*).
Having uttered the exclamation with the final word [of the hymn], "With his kinsmen" (*sa-jātebhiḥ*), he recites the *nivid*.
Having recited that [hymn] by quarters, he then recites the *sūdadohas* verse.
Then he recites the manifest *bṛhatī*s;
with those which remain from the twenty-five, he begins.
ŚŚS 18.10.3: "vayam gha tvā sutāvantaḥ" consists of fifteen [verses].
ŚŚS 18.10.4: These twenty [verses] are *bṛhatī*s in their manifest form (*pratyakṣa*). ŚŚS 18.10.5: Now follow the *pragāthas*.
Of those six [verses], he proceeds with the three that remain:
"He who is the king of the peoples" (yo rājā carṣaṇīnām) is three verses; "Him, the wondrous one, the subduer of enemies" (tam vo dasmam ṛtīṣaham) is one verse.
ŚŚS 18.10.9: "ā no viśvāsu havya" and so forth—three [verses]. ŚŚS 18.10.10: "tvām id ā hyo naraḥ" and so forth—four [verses]. ŚŚS 18.10.11: Now, the hymns of the Vālakhilyas are six.
ŚŚS 18.10.12: Of these, he omits two *pragāthas*, namely the *indra-nihava* and the *vaiśvadeva*, [beginning with] "ā no viśve sajoṣasaḥ.
ŚŚS 18.10.13: Those [remaining] are forty *pragāthas*.
ŚŚS 18.11.1: Then he recites the *bṛhatīs* that are directly perceived.

ŚŚS 18.11.2: *matsy apāyi te mahaḥ*, *asmā asmā id andhaso balaṃ dhehi tanūṣu naḥ*, *yujāno haritā rathe*, *tava id indra aham āśasā*, *amāsu pakvam airaya*, *iyam yā nīcy arkiṇī*, *pra te ratham mithūkṛtam antaryaccha jighāṃsataḥ*, *tvaṃ viśvasya jagataḥ*—these are the ten *ekapātinī* verses. ŚŚS 18.11.3: *ayaṃ te astu haryataḥ*, *ā mandair indra haribhiḥ*—these two hymns (*sūkta*).
ŚŚS 18.11.4: Having recited those [hymns] by half-verses (*ardharcaśas*), one then recites the *sūdadohas* verse.
ŚŚS 18.12.1: He begins with the *aśīti* consisting of an *auṣṇiha* verse: "indraḥ suteṣu someṣu. ŚŚS 18.12.2:
These consist of eleven triplets (*tṛca*). ŚŚS 18.12.3:
Of the eleven [verses] beginning with "ya indra somapātama," he omits one, namely "indram vṛtrāya hantave."
"Sing forth unto him" (*tam v abhi pra gāyata*)—these are four [verses].
"O friends, let us pray for blessings" (*sakhāya ā śiṣāmahi*)—these are nine.
"He who alone bestows wealth" (*ya eka id vidayate*) and "Come hither to the pressed juice" (*ā yāhy adribhiḥ sutam*)—these are two triplets (*tṛca*).
Those are thirty-six triplets.
Then he recites four hundred *gāyatrī* verses;
"No one is superior to you, O Indra," consists of six [verses].
ŚŚS 18.13.3: "divaś cid gha duhitaram" consists of fourteen verses;
ŚŚS 18.13.4: "ā tu na indra vṛtrahan" consists of twenty-one verses;
ŚŚS 18.13.5: "ā va indram krivim yathā," "yad indra aham," and "yathā tvam" consist of fifteen verses each.
"pra saṃrājaṃ carṣaṇīnām ut tvā mandantu stomāḥ"—this [hymn] consists of twelve verses.
"ā pra drava parāvataḥ"—this consists of nine verses.
Thus, there are four hundred *gāyatrī* verses.
ŚŚS 18.13.9: "vayam u tvām apūrvyā" and so forth are eight *kākubha* *pragāthas*.
ŚŚS 18.13.10: "indrāya sāma gāyata" and so forth constitute the whole [of the *sāman*]. ŚŚS 18.13.11: Having recited that by half-verses, [one recites] the *sūdadohas* verse from here on.
Now he recites this Vaśa hymn by half-verses: "O Lord of many riches, one such as you... (RV 8.97.1). Its seventeenth verse is a Jagatī; that he recites by quarters.
Now, the twenty-first, twenty-second, and twenty-fourth [verses] are *paṅkti*s; one should recite them by their *paṅkti* structure.
Regarding the five-footed verse beginning "A hundredfold to the Dāsa Balbūtha," one should pause after combining three of its feet and proceed with the next two.
The thirteenth and thirtieth verses are *dvipadā*s; having recited these foot by foot, one then recites the *sūdadohas*.
Then these two expanded half-verses, and then the *sūdadohas* verse;
that [verse] is then released from there.
At this point, the reciter has recited twenty-four times.
ŚŚS 18.15.1: Then he recites these two-footed verses (dvipadās).
ŚŚS 18.15.2: "imā nu kam bhuvanā sīṣadhāma" and so on, five verses.
ŚŚS 18.15.3: "ā yāhi vanasā saha," four verses.
"‘This is the Brahman who is seasonal’—these are three [verses].
‘Sing forth a song for Indra, the greatest slayer of Vṛtra, O sages, that he may enjoy it!
The Maruts, skilled in praise, sing their hymn; the famous youth Indra utters his response.’"
Dwelling in the honey-sweet offering, may we prosper and obtain wealth, O Indra.
From every side, O Giver, bring it to us from every side, you whom we implore as the most powerful one.
You are the best leader, the most excellent dancer, and the self-ruler; you are the most bountiful for the winning of booty.

"For you alone, O Bounteous One, rule over wealth from of old with unassailable might"—these are six [verses]. "Upon the yokes for him, the one [thrusts] the thunderbolt; may we win the strength ordained by the gods"—these are twenty-one two-footed verses; they are recited foot by foot.

ŚŚS 18.16.1: Then he recites this hymn dedicated to Indra and Agni, the *śaṃsa* consisting of *gāyatrī* verses, beginning with "O Indra and Agni, you two [are] for us well... (indrāgnī yuvam su naḥ). ŚŚS 18.16.2: Its second verse consists of seven padas; of that, he makes the first an *anuṣṭubh* and the latter a *gāyatrī* *śaṃsa*.
ŚŚS 18.16.3: The final verse is a *triṣṭubh*; he recites it by feet (*pacchas*).
Now he recites this insertion (*āvapana*):
"For you, O Indra, this honey is poured out"—this is one verse;
"To the all-conqueror, the winner of wealth, the winner of light"—these are six verses.
ŚŚS 18.17.4: Those [verses] are recited by pādas.

ŚŚS 18.17.5: "svādor itthā viṣūvataḥ" is a triplet in the Paṅkti meter; that is the Paṅkti-śaṃsa. ŚŚS 18.17.6: "pra vo mahe mahivr̥dhe bharadhvam" is a triplet in the Vairāja meter; that is recited half-verse by half-verse.
ŚŚS 18.17.7: "praty asmai pipīṣate"—this triplet in the *anuṣṭubh* meter is recited half-verse by half-verse.
ŚŚS 18.18.1: Then he recites this collection of *anuṣṭubh* verses. ŚŚS 18.18.2: "ehi stomān abhisvara"—these nine [verses].
"Indram viśvā avīvṛdhan" and so on are eight [verses]. "Asāvi soma indra te" and so on are six.
"Ā nas te gantu matsaraḥ" and so on are four.
ŚŚS 18.18.5: "matsi no vasya iṣṭaye," five verses;
ŚŚS 18.18.6: "yas te sādhiṣṭho 'vase," seven verses;
ŚŚS 18.18.7: "uro ṣ ṭa indra rādhasaḥ," two verses.
ŚŚS 18.18.8: "O Indra, whose rain is wonderful"—these four [verses].
ŚŚS 18.18.9: "He who is the giver of wealth, O most wealthy one"—these six [verses].
ŚŚS 18.18.10: "Come hither, O Indra, with your bay horses"—these fifteen [verses].
ŚŚS 18.18.11: "sa pratnathā kavivṛdhaḥ"—this triplet;
ŚŚS 18.18.12: "yaj jāyathā apūrvyaḥ"—these two verses;
ŚŚS 18.18.13: "ā tvā giro rathīr iva"—the whole [hymn].

ŚŚS 18.18.14: "Śāsa itthā mahān asi" and so on, [reciting] the whole [hymn]. ŚŚS 18.18.15: That [he recites] by half-verses. ŚŚS 18.19.1: Then he recites this [hymn] consisting of one hundred *triṣṭubh* verses.
And this *Hairaṇyastūpīya*;
and this *Yātīya*;
and this *Sajanīya*.
"O Adhvaryus,
bring Soma for Indra," and the two hymns beginning with "Come hither, standing upon the chariot-seat; you are the warrior, the bull,
the self-ruling king," and the triplet beginning with "Thee, the most heroic among men, with songs and hymns."
ŚŚS 18.19.8: [He recites] "The truthful Maghavan, the impetuous one, shall come," and so on for the whole [hymn].
ŚŚS 18.19.9: [He recites] the two hymns "O Indra, a seat has been prepared for you" and "Upward the prayers.

ŚŚS 18.19.10: Therein, before the hymn beginning with "Upward the prayers," he recites the word-appendages (pada-anuṣaṅga): having uttered the first half-verse of the triplet beginning with "He who made the crossing-roads tremble," he stops.
ŚŚS 18.20.1: Then, having joined the first foot of the second [verse] with the third foot of the first, he pronounces the *praṇava*.
ŚŚS 18.20.2: Then, having joined the second foot of the second [verse] with the last foot of the first, he pauses.
ŚŚS 18.20.3: Then, having joined the first foot of the last [verse] with the third foot of the second, he pronounces the *praṇava*.
ŚŚS 18.20.4: Then, having joined the second foot of the second [verse] with the last foot of the first, he pauses.
ŚŚS 18.20.5: Then, with the remaining portion by half-verses, he chants the *praṇava*.
ŚŚS 18.20.6: Then, leaving aside the last [verse] of the *udbrahmīya*, he calls out.

He concludes with the *paridhānīyā* verse recited three times. Having concluded, he mutters the *ukthavīrya* formula: first that belonging to the one-day (*aikāhika*) sacrifice, and then that belonging to the *mahāvrata*. [The formula is: "Great art thou; glory art thou; splendor art thou; enjoyment art thou; thou art one who enjoys; become for my enjoyment. This same [formula] applies when the *sūdadohas* verse has been recited once, up until the *upasarjanī* vessel is being counted during the recitation, excluding the silent recitation (*tūṣṇīṃśaṃsa*). Thus, it amounts to a thousand *bṛhatī* verses.
He calls thrice: for the *stotriya*, the *nivid*, and the *paridhānīyā*. The two *yājyās* are identical.
ŚŚS 18.21.5: They loosen the swing even before the *vaṣaṭ* call has been uttered.
ŚŚS 18.21.6: While still holding the cup, he descends from it facing eastward.
ŚŚS 18.21.7: He pushes back the plank of the swing toward the west.
Touching the cup, he mutters: "Whatever I have failed to win in this progeny, may I win that after it.
Having sought the invitation from the Adhvaryu, he consumes [the draught] with the formula: "For vigor, thee!
This is the Atigrāhya cup for Viśvakarman.

ŚŚS 18.21.11: "May the marrow-drinkers come to me; may they drink with the fat; may the inspired thoughts drink with me. Beholding my dear body, I take delight in it. For the vigor of the gods, I [take] you. ŚŚS 18.21.12: Then they consume the cups [with the formula]: "You are a god, O Narāśaṃsa. ŚŚS 18.21.13: The midday pressing has been prepared.
ŚŚS 18.22.1: Now, therefore, follows the third pressing (tṛtīyasavana).
ŚŚS 18.22.2: The two triplets, "tat savitur vṛṇīmahe" and "adyā no deva savitar," are the introductory and following verses for the Vaiśvadeva [śastra].
ŚŚS 18.22.3: This indeed is the constant extension (ātāna) of the one-day sacrifice (ekāha).
"Of that god Savitṛ, the desirable [gift] is great"—this is the verse addressed to Savitṛ.
"For they two, Heaven and Earth, are the benefactors of all"—this is the verse addressed to Heaven and Earth.
"What indeed has the most excellent one, what has the youngest not come to us?"—this is the verse addressed to the Ṛbhus.

"Of this lovely, grey-haired Hotṛ..."—this is the *salila* verse for the Viśvedevas; "From the ocean they flow forth; this water is common to all"—these [two verses] he recites half-verse by half-verse, and the others foot by foot.
Having recited that, he places the *nivid* with the "A no bhadra" hymn.
The *paridhānīyā* (concluding verse) is the one beginning with "pañca janāḥ."
Thus, indeed, is the Vaiśvadeva.
Now, therefore, follows the Āgnimāruta.
"To Vaiśvānara of broad radiance, the sage..."—this is the Vaiśvānariya hymn.
"O Maruts, eager for sacrifice, with brilliant aspects"—this is the hymn for the Maruts.
If they should perform the *yajñāyajñīya* as the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*, its *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses are those prescribed in the *uktha*.
For these two, the *śastra* recitation is as previously ordained.
ŚŚS 18.23.6: Or alternatively, if they chant the *iḷāda*, the three-verse *stotriya* is "O Agni, your fame and vigor," and the next [verse] from that same hymn serves as the *anurūpa*.
ŚŚS 18.23.7: Or if they should chant on the entire six-verse hymn, one should make "Neither Agni nor with our own prayers" its *anurūpa* consisting of six verses.
The *śastra* is recited verse by half-verse (*ardharcaśas*).
Or, if they should perform it in *aticchandas* meters, the *stotriya* triplet is "I consider Agni the Hotṛ, the bountiful one," and the following [triplet] is the *anurūpa* from that same hymn.
That which was the seventh verse of the hymn, he makes the third; that is the *anurūpa*.

"ayam jāyata manuṣo dharīmaṇi"—this triplet is the stotra-verse; for this very reason, the following verse serves as its *anurūpa* (corresponding verse). The *śastra* (recitation) consists of four verses.
In this case, one should not recite the *yoni* (source-verse) of the *yajñāyajñīya*.
ŚŚS 18.23.14: "baḷ itthā tad vapuṣe dhāyi darśatam" is the verse addressed to Jātavedas. ŚŚS 18.23.15: These are the hymns for the Āgnimāruta [rite].
ŚŚS 18.23.16: These are the hymns for this day.
Thus the Agniṣṭoma is completed.
They dwell for that night.
Then, in the morning, they enter upon the Udayanīya Atirātra.
ŚŚS 18.24.2: That which is the *prāyaṇīya* [opening] sacrifice is indeed the *udayanīya* [concluding] sacrifice.
ŚŚS 18.24.3: Having crowded together all the ritual implements there, the Maitrāvaruṇa priest issues the call.
ŚŚS 18.24.4: They wear either the garments of those consecrated for the first month.
They set those aside for the nine-night sacrifice and for the final month;
then, for the other months, they wear either skins or wet garments.
For in that [day], the rites are performed once they have been concluded.
They do not take up the *vasatīvarī* waters from the following day. He does not utter the *atipraiṣa* call.
They offer the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations;
they proceed to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*);
the ritual of the purificatory bath is performed.

ŚŚS 18.24.14: If they are going to eat in the sacrificial halls, they should indeed set up the swing-altar (preṅkha) together with the other materials. ŚŚS 18.24.15: But if they intend to burn [the remains], it should remain right here.
ŚŚS 18.24.16: The purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) is well-known [from the standard ritual].
The *udayanīyā* offering is well known;
the *anūbandhyā* offering is well known.
When the omentum of that [animal] has been offered, having enclosed a small portion from the southwestern part of the altar and sitting upon it, they have their hair and beards shaved.
They clip all their body hairs and nails;
they bathe;
they adorn themselves.
They arrange the turban by way of producing the hair;
they complete the remainder for the Anūbandhyā cow;
it concludes with the heart-spit.
When that [offering] has been completed, they consign the fires as they were distributed and go out between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*.

Having prepared the fire-places to the north, sprinkled them with water, smeared them with cow-dung, churned out the fires, spread them out, and brought forward the *praṇītā* waters, they offer the full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*). Those who have maintained their sacred fires perform the concluding sacrifices (*udavasānīyā*) separately.
Now, those who have not maintained their sacred fires wait upon the householder alone.
ŚŚS 18.24.29: He may indeed perform the *pṛṣṭha-śamanīya* sacrifice according to his desire.
ŚŚS 18.24.30: Or he may not perform it at all according to his desire.
ŚŚS 18.24.31: But if he should perform it, these very same officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) of his *sattra* shall serve as the priests for this rite.
ŚŚS 18.24.32: To them he should give whatever is to be given.
ŚŚS 18.24.33: Here the year comes to a conclusion. ŚŚS 18.24.34: Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the offices of the Hotṛ priests.
From that, from that, of his.
